cards.front: Define an agentic AI system in one sentence.
cards.back: A distributed system with a nondeterministic component in the control path. Distributed means timeouts, retries, tracing; nondeterministic means evals; in the control path means injection is privilege escalation.
cards.hook: Every requirement falls out of that one line

cards.front: The published number on multi-agent token cost.
cards.back: Anthropic's multi-agent research system consumed roughly 15x the tokens of a single chat interaction. Worth it for open-ended parallelizable research; explicitly not for tightly-coupled shared-context tasks.
cards.hook: 15x, and they said when not to

cards.front: Anthropic's published ordering for agent patterns.
cards.back: Start simplest: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Add autonomy only when the task genuinely needs open-ended decisions.
cards.hook: Simplest possible, then increase

cards.front: Name the five points on the autonomy spectrum, in order.
cards.back: Prompt, chain, workflow, agent, multi-agent. Left to right you trade determinism for delegated control: debuggable and cheap becomes hard and expensive with compounding risk.
cards.hook: Every notch up costs determinism

cards.front: Why does the model being in the control path change the security model?
cards.back: A model producing content badly makes bad content. A model deciding what happens next, when manipulated, executes an attacker's plan using your credentials.
cards.hook: Content bug versus privilege escalation

cards.front: Why are state, observability, evals and security drawn as cross-cutting?
cards.back: Because anything drawn as a box in the flow gets built later, and later never comes. Cross-cutting means every layer carries it from the start.
cards.hook: A box means "we'll add it before GA"

cards.front: What do you get from multi-agent adopted for org-chart reasons?
cards.back: A distributed monolith with a language model as the message bus — all the coordination cost, none of the parallelism.
cards.hook: The org chart is not the architecture

cards.front: DPD and the Chevrolet dealership: the same two missing gates.
cards.back: Scope enforcement on input and policy validation on output. One chatbot swore and disparaged its own company; the other agreed to sell a Tahoe for $1 as 'legally binding'.
cards.hook: No concept of authorized statements

cards.front: The five gaps between a demo and production.
cards.back: Input distribution, failure surface, scale economics, consequence, and time. When someone says it worked in the demo, ask which gap the demo did not cross.
cards.hook: "It worked in the demo" names the gap

cards.front: At 200K runs a month, what does per-run cost mean?
cards.back: A 3-cent design is $6K a month; a 30-cent design is $60K. In a demo of 20 runs the difference is invisible, which is why demos never surface it.
cards.hook: Ten cents of design, $54K of bill

cards.front: What does the 'time' gap mean for a system that works today?
cards.back: It runs for 18 months while the model, the prompt, the docs and the APIs all drift underneath it. Nothing you validated stays validated.
cards.hook: Eighteen months of drift under a fixed prompt

cards.front: What must a multi-agent handoff specify?
cards.back: Which agent owns the next step, the typed payload, the expected output schema, the timeout, and the conflict-resolution rule. Undefined handoffs are where multi-agent systems die.
cards.hook: Five fields, or it dies at the seam

cards.front: State the spectrum design rule and its real justification.
cards.back: Choose the leftmost point that solves the problem — not out of caution, but to conserve your debugging budget for the parts that genuinely need nondeterminism.
cards.hook: Spend nondeterminism where it pays

cards.front: What shape are most production 'agents' actually?
cards.back: Workflows with two or three agentic decision points. That is the correct shape for the overwhelming majority of enterprise use cases.
cards.hook: Structure is not the opposite of autonomy

cards.front: Why is multi-agent structurally more expensive, mechanically?
cards.back: Each agent re-reads context, so context is paid for repeatedly. Add handoff overhead and often-serialized waits, and cost plus latency grow faster than the work does.
cards.hook: Context billed once per agent

cards.front: When does multi-agent earn its keep?
cards.back: When at least two hold: genuine parallelism, genuine specialization with different tools or permissions, adversarial review, or different lifecycles.
cards.hook: Two of four, or collapse it

cards.front: The six-agent change assistant: what did collapsing it recover?
cards.back: p95 fell from 90 seconds, latency dropped about 70% and cost about 80%, and the trace became one linear thing a human can read.
cards.hook: Six workflow IDs, nobody accountable

cards.front: Which multi-agent justification is architectural rather than stylistic?
cards.back: Different credentials. A read-only investigator and a change-approved remediator genuinely differ in permissions — that is a boundary, not a preference.
cards.hook: Different credentials is a real boundary
cards.aryaka: Diagnosis agents read MyAryaka; only a separately-credentialed remediator may push config.

cards.front: When steps are known and fixed, what is the implementation?
cards.back: Plain functions. Genuinely plain functions — no graph runtime, no framework, no orchestration layer to debug.
cards.hook: Plain functions, genuinely

cards.front: Where does the policy engine sit, and why does the position matter?
cards.back: Between the model and the tools — never inside the model's reasoning. The model proposes, deterministic code disposes. That one structural choice prevents a whole category of incidents.
cards.hook: Between model and tools, not inside

cards.front: The four-stage action chain, in order.
cards.back: Model proposes, code validates, human approves, tool executes. Skipping the validate stage is what turns a wrong proposal into a wrong action.
cards.hook: Four stages; the model owns one

cards.front: At high concurrency, what becomes the system's bottleneck?
cards.back: Model provider rate limits. You need a queue and a degradation policy, not just retries — retry storms against a rate limit make it worse.
cards.hook: Retries against a limit deepen it

cards.front: Name the layers of the reference architecture in order.
cards.back: Ingress and scope gate, orchestration, then model / context-RAG / approval-policy in parallel, then tools, then systems of record.
cards.hook: Scope gate first, systems of record last

cards.front: Resumability gives crash recovery and day-long approval waits. What is the third win?
cards.back: Replaying a production failure locally against a fixed state — the closest thing to a stack trace an agent gets.
cards.hook: Replay production locally

cards.front: Many teams, many workflows — what changes?
cards.back: A shared orchestration platform with common middleware: auth, tracing, cost accounting, eval hooks, policy engine. Otherwise every team reimplements all of it, differently and worse.
cards.hook: Reimplemented differently and worse

cards.front: The one-line test for a fake multi-agent system.
cards.back: If you can draw it as a straight line, it is not multi-agent — it is a pipeline you made expensive.
cards.hook: Straight line means pipeline

cards.front: The three caps every loop needs, and the fourth thing.
cards.back: Max steps, max cost, max wall-clock — and log which cap fired. A loop with no cap is an outage waiting for an unusual input, and unusual inputs arrive daily at scale.
cards.hook: Cap three things, log which fired

cards.front: State the orchestration selection rule.
cards.back: Pick the weakest orchestration primitive that works: pipeline, then state machine, then graph, then durable workflow engine, then autonomous loop.
cards.hook: Weakest primitive that works

cards.front: What forces a durable workflow engine specifically?
cards.back: Long-running work that must survive crashes and deploys, needs exactly-once semantics, or waits days on a human. Temporal or Step Functions, not a graph runtime.
cards.hook: Days-long waits need durability

cards.front: The test for whether your control flow is explicit enough.
cards.back: A production agent's flow should be drawable on a whiteboard. If it can't be drawn, it can't be reviewed, and nobody knows what it does under an unusual input.
cards.hook: Undrawable means unreviewable

cards.front: When does agentic RAG earn its cost over standard RAG?
cards.back: When the task is multi-step, needs decomposition, spans multiple systems, or depends on intermediate findings. "When can I get a replacement" needs order, product and delivery systems.
cards.hook: Four triggers, not "it's complex"

cards.front: In a design round, what is the first move on any question?
cards.back: Name the category the question belongs to — platform architecture, security, retrieval trade-off. The surface question is rarely what is being tested.
cards.hook: Reframe before you answer

cards.front: What separates a senior design answer from a correct one?
cards.back: Explicitly naming the trade-off you accepted. Structure, example, then the cost you knowingly took. Candidates skip the fourth move.
cards.hook: The fourth move is the signal

cards.front: The agent keeps calling the wrong tool. What kind of defect is that?
cards.back: A tool-design defect. Vague descriptions, overlapping responsibilities, weak parameter schemas, missing usage examples. Fix boundaries, schemas, enums and validation — not the model.
cards.hook: "We cannot just train the model"

cards.front: Walk the trajectory — what six things do you inspect, in order?
cards.back: User input, planning step, tool selected, generated arguments, tool response, final answer. Debugging anywhere else is guessing.
cards.hook: Six stops, in order

cards.front: A2A — what problem does it solve that MCP doesn't?
cards.back: Sold as: agents talking to agents | Actually: Google's cross-vendor protocol where an agent card advertises skills, auth and endpoints so agents can delegate tasks; MCP is agent-to-tool, A2A is agent-to-agent | Changes: cross-vendor delegation with long-running task callbacks becomes possible | Say: "MCP plus A2A is the complete interop story — tools and peers."
cards.hook: Agent cards, not tool schemas

cards.front: Agent harness — what is it, precisely?
cards.back: Sold as: the magic wrapper that makes models agentic | Actually: the deterministic runtime around the model: context assembly, memory, tool runtime, loop control, budgets, trace | Changes: you stop shipping prompts and start versioning a runtime | Say: "The model is rented; the harness is owned."
cards.hook: Nine boxes around one rented model
cards.aryaka: Our ticket copilot's harness outlives whichever frontier model we're on this quarter.

cards.front: When is it a workflow and not an agent?
cards.back: Sold as: everything is an agent now | Actually: if the control flow is known in advance, it is a workflow; agents are for when the next step depends on what the last one found | Changes: you stop paying agent tax on deterministic pipelines | Say: "The path is known here, so it's a workflow with LLM steps."
cards.hook: Unknown control flow is the only reason

cards.front: AgentOps — what is it beyond LLMOps?
cards.back: Sold as: observability built for agents | Actually: run-level tracing — trajectories, per-run cost, tool-error rates, termination distributions, time-travel replay | Changes: the vendor question, not the decision to instrument; pick one that also carries evals | Say: "Request dashboards can't see a 40-step run going nowhere."
cards.hook: Trace tools without evals strand you
cards.aryaka: Braintrust, LangSmith, Phoenix, Datadog LLM, AgentOps — the eval flywheel is the differentiator.

cards.front: AI gateway — what does putting one in front buy you?
cards.back: Sold as: one endpoint for every model | Actually: a single fronting endpoint doing caching, cost caps, per-team attribution, provider fallback and retries | Changes: cost control and vendor swap become configuration, not code changes | Say: "Cloudflare's runs at a 30-40% cache hit rate — that's the lever."
cards.hook: One seam, every model behind it

cards.front: Autonomy spectrum — how do you use it in a design round?
cards.back: Sold as: build an autonomous agent | Actually: a ladder from scripted workflow to full autonomy; you pick the leftmost point that solves the problem and justify why not simpler | Changes: 'agent' becomes a defended choice instead of a default | Say: "What's the simplest point that solves this — and why not simpler?"
cards.hook: Leftmost that works, defended
cards.aryaka: Tier-1 triage sits at plan-then-approve; only diagnosis is agentic, remediation isn't.

cards.front: Budgets as a first-class object — what does that mean in code?
cards.back: Sold as: we cap spend | Actually: a typed object capping steps, tokens, cost and wall-clock that nests into sub-agents | Changes: a runaway is impossible by construction, not by vigilance | Say: "Budgets live in the harness, not in the prompt. Prompts don't enforce."
cards.hook: A prompt cannot enforce a ceiling
cards.aryaka: Per-tenant budget objects stop one noisy customer eating the support-agent's day.

cards.front: Compaction — what is it and what is the catch?
cards.back: Sold as: summarize the history to save tokens | Actually: summarizing a run's transcript into a fixed schema so the run continues inside the window | Changes: compaction becomes a model call you must eval — it can hallucinate | Say: "Raw transcript still goes to the trace; compaction is never deletion."
cards.hook: A summarizer that lies is durable

cards.front: Consolidation — what runs, when, and on what?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent learns over time | Actually: a batch job distilling episodic events into durable semantic facts — offline, not per-turn | Changes: memory quality becomes a scheduled pipeline with an owner | Say: "Consolidation is batch. Anything writing semantic memory inline is a bug."
cards.hook: Sleep, not thinking

cards.front: Context engineering — what is the actual job?
cards.back: Sold as: prompt engineering, grown up | Actually: deciding per step what enters a finite window: system prompt, retrieved docs, history, tool results — and what gets left out | Changes: context becomes a budget you allocate, not a bucket you fill | Say: "Every token in the window displaced another token. Show me the assembly policy."
cards.hook: Assembly is subtraction, not addition

cards.front: Context rot — mechanism, not vibe.
cards.back: Sold as: long context is solved, just use the bigger window | Actually: attention dilutes as context grows — quality degrades while nothing errors | Changes: you cap and compact instead of buying a bigger window | Say: "It's silent: no exception, no alert, just worse answers."
cards.hook: The silent quality killer
cards.aryaka: A 30-tool single agent for NOC triage rots; four scoped workers don't.

cards.front: Deterministic replay — what is being replayed?
cards.back: Sold as: reproduce the bug | Actually: re-running the harness against recorded model outputs, so harness logic is testable without the model | Changes: harness bugs get unit tests; only behaviour needs evals | Say: "Mock the model, assert the loop. Evals test behaviour, tests test code."
cards.hook: Mock the model, keep the loop honest

cards.front: Distillation and small models — when does it pay?
cards.back: Sold as: small models are cheaper, use them | Actually: training a student to mimic a teacher on a narrow task; it loses general capability, and below ~500 requests/day the $200-500 training cost never amortizes | Changes: volume and narrowness decide it, not model fashion | Say: "Narrow, high-volume, stable task — otherwise stay on the API."
cards.hook: Below 500/day the math never closes

cards.front: Goal condition — why is it not 'the model says done'?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent knows when it's finished | Actually: a deterministic check that the task actually succeeded — file written, ticket updated, config validated | Changes: you get a success signal that cannot be talked into existence | Say: "'Done' is a claim. A goal condition is a verification."
cards.hook: Verify the artifact, not the sentence

cards.front: GraphRAG — how does it differ from what we call KG-RAG?
cards.back: Sold as: RAG that finally understands relationships | Actually: an entity graph plus pre-summarized communities; 72% comprehensiveness win over vector RAG, 97% fewer tokens on global summaries | Changes: indexing cost fell from $33K to under $5 per corpus with LazyGraphRAG | Say: "Hybrid first; add graph where traces prove structural retrieval failure."
cards.hook: The 2024 cost objection is dead
cards.aryaka: 'Which customers share the device model behind last month's flaps' is a traversal, not a similarity search.

cards.front: Groundedness — precisely what is being scored?
cards.back: Sold as: hallucination score | Actually: whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context — scored independently of whether the answer is liked | Changes: retrieval quality and synthesis quality get measured separately | Say: "Fluent, relevant, and ungrounded is the dangerous quadrant."
cards.hook: Supported by context, or invented

cards.front: GRPO — what kind of thing is it?
cards.back: Sold as: the trick behind reasoning models | Actually: sample a group of answers, score each against the group average, drop PPO's critic — cheaper, stabler RL | Changes: nothing operationally; it is a weights lever, we consume its output | Say: "Training-time method. Our lever is the harness, not the weights."
cards.hook: DeepSeek-R1's method, not our knob

cards.front: Guardrails — why is 'guardrails on a model' the wrong frame?
cards.back: Sold as: bolt safety onto the model | Actually: a harness is closer to an operating system for a process that cannot be trusted to manage itself — guardrails are one hook inside it | Changes: you stop shopping for a guardrail product to fix an architecture problem | Say: "Guardrails are hooks in a runtime. The runtime is the control."
cards.hook: An OS, not a fence

cards.front: Harness engineering — what discipline is it replacing?
cards.back: Sold as: the successor to prompt engineering | Actually: investing in the code around the model rather than the wording inside it — memory schema, loop policy, tool contracts, eval set | Changes: budget and headcount move from prompt tuning to runtime engineering | Say: "Frontier models converge and change under us; the harness is the durable asset."
cards.hook: Prompts are text. Harnesses are systems.

cards.front: Approval UX in a long-running loop — the architectural requirement.
cards.back: Sold as: add a human in the loop | Actually: approval must suspend and persist, never block a thread; plus notification, a visible pending queue, a TTL, and time-to-decide as a metric | Changes: hours-long waits stop leaking orphaned workflows | Say: "Above 95% approval rate it's theater — shrink what needs a human."
cards.hook: No TTL means orphaned workflows

cards.front: LLM-as-a-judge — where is it legitimate?
cards.back: Sold as: automated quality scoring at scale | Actually: a scored rubric (groundedness, relevance, tone) usable as one mechanism among several — never the only one, and never its own regression gate | Changes: you keep human review and deterministic checks in the mix | Say: "Judges drift with the model that runs them. We anchor with human samples."
cards.hook: A judge you never audit is a rumor

cards.front: LLMOps versus MLOps — what is genuinely different?
cards.back: Sold as: MLOps with a new logo | Actually: the outer loop: failure clusters become eval cases, eval cases become prompt/harness fixes, shipped weekly | Changes: your roadmap is the failure-cluster distribution, not a backlog | Say: "Our velocity metric is time from eval case to shipped fix."
cards.hook: Failure clusters are the roadmap

cards.front: Loop engineering — what is actually being engineered?
cards.back: Sold as: making the agent smarter each iteration | Actually: iteration and termination policy: when to continue, when to stop, and which of the seven termination mechanisms fired | Changes: you own a stopping policy, not a hope that it stops | Say: "Capability without loop engineering looks agentic and doesn't finish tasks."
cards.hook: AutoGPT had the model, not the loop

cards.front: MCP — what it standardizes and what it does not.
cards.back: Sold as: plug any tool into any agent, securely | Actually: Model Context Protocol standardizes how tools and context are exposed to agents — the interface, not the security model | Changes: you still own auth, tenancy and blast radius per tool | Say: "MCP removed our integration tax. It did not give us authorization."
cards.hook: Standard interface, your security model

cards.front: Memory-need gate — what does it save?
cards.back: Sold as: always retrieve context | Actually: a router deciding whether a query needs retrieval at all | Changes: most trivial turns skip retrieval, cutting latency and tokens | Say: "Half our turns need no retrieval. Gating them is free latency."
cards.hook: Retrieval is a decision, not a reflex

cards.front: Memory poisoning — why is it worse than prompt injection?
cards.back: Sold as: an injection variant | Actually: planting a durable false fact — persistent prompt injection that survives the session and every later retrieval | Changes: writes need provenance and review, not just reads needing filters | Say: "One bad write, every future run wrong. Injection ends with the session."
cards.hook: Injection with a shelf life
cards.aryaka: A wrong 'ACME uses IPsec not SSL' fact would mis-route tickets for months.

cards.front: The memory taxonomy — three kinds and their write rules.
cards.back: Sold as: give the agent memory | Actually: episodic (append-only log), semantic (distilled durable facts), procedural (instructions and skills, version-controlled as code) | Changes: each kind gets its own write path, TTL and review policy | Say: "Procedural memory is code — it goes through review, not through a chat turn."
cards.hook: Three stores, three write policies

cards.front: Model cascade — what makes it work rather than just cheap?
cards.back: Sold as: route cheap requests to a cheap model | Actually: tiered routing with an escalation rule and a measured escalation rate; savings come from the tier mix, safety from the escalation path | Changes: you own a routing policy and its accuracy, not just a model list | Say: "Cascade is only cheap if escalation is rare and correct — we measure both."
cards.hook: Savings live in the escalation rate

cards.front: Oscillation detection — what exactly do you detect?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent got stuck | Actually: repeated actions without progress — detected by hashing (tool, arguments) and catching repeats | Changes: a cheap deterministic check replaces a model-judged 'is it stuck' | Say: "Hash the action, not the text. Three identical hashes, terminate."
cards.hook: Same call three times is not thinking

cards.front: Progressive disclosure of skills — what loads when?
cards.back: Sold as: give the agent all its tools | Actually: skill metadata always in context; the body loaded only on demand | Changes: adding the 40th skill stops costing every request tokens | Say: "Names and one-liners are cheap; bodies are on demand."
cards.hook: Index always, chapters on request

cards.front: Prompt caching — what you must do to your prompt to earn it.
cards.back: Sold as: 50-90% cheaper input tokens | Actually: the provider caches a stable prefix — so the stable system prompt and tool definitions go first, variable content last | Changes: prompt ordering becomes a cost decision, and rewrites become expensive | Say: "Any edit to the prefix invalidates the cache for everyone."
cards.hook: Stable prefix first, or no discount

cards.front: Prompt injection — why call it privilege escalation?
cards.back: Sold as: a jailbreak problem | Actually: untrusted text reaching a model that holds tool credentials — the exploit is the tool permission, not the wording | Changes: the fix is least-privilege tools and gated side effects, not a better system prompt | Say: "Treat model output as untrusted input to every tool it can call."
cards.hook: The credential is the vulnerability
cards.aryaka: A customer-pasted log line is untrusted input to any config-write tool.

cards.front: Sandboxing an agent — what does it actually constrain?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent runs safely | Actually: the agent cannot write outside a configured root or execute outside an allowed command set; policy is central, enforcement is local | Changes: policy becomes a versioned file distributed by git, not per-team negotiation | Say: "Central policy file, sandbox enforcement, no per-team exceptions."
cards.hook: Policy in git, enforcement in the sandbox

cards.front: Semantic cache — the layer, and its failure mode.
cards.back: Sold as: cut cost by caching similar questions | Actually: an L2 layer serving near-match queries from cache; its failure is serving a stale operational fact after the underlying state changed | Changes: cacheability becomes a per-fact-class decision with invalidation | Say: "We cache explanations, never live device state."
cards.hook: Near-match plus stale fact equals outage
cards.aryaka: A cached MTU threshold two days stale is a black-holed site, not a saved dollar.

cards.front: Spec-driven development — what changes in the workflow?
cards.back: Sold as: write a spec, the agent builds it | Actually: an executable version-controlled spec is the source of truth, code is regenerable output | Changes: review moves from diff to intent; GitHub reports ~10x fewer regenerate-from-scratch cycles | Say: "Same move as plan-before-execute, applied to code."
cards.hook: Approve the intent, regenerate the diff

cards.front: Speculative decoding — what does it change and not change?
cards.back: Sold as: 2-3x faster inference | Actually: a draft model proposes tokens the target verifies in parallel — a latency win on latency-bound workloads with no quality loss | Changes: it is a throughput knob on self-hosted or managed endpoints, not a cost redesign | Say: "Latency-bound, not cost-bound. It won't fix a token-volume problem."
cards.hook: Free latency, no quality trade

cards.front: Sub-agent delegation — when is it the right move?
cards.back: Sold as: a team of specialist agents | Actually: handing a bounded sub-problem its own context window and budget, inside a deterministic outer workflow | Changes: it becomes context isolation, not an org chart | Say: "Last resort, bounded scope, own budget — not a swarm."
cards.hook: Isolation of context, not a hierarchy
cards.aryaka: One investigation sub-agent per alert, capped; the outer NOC flow stays deterministic.

cards.front: Supersession — why not just overwrite the fact?
cards.back: Sold as: keep memory current | Actually: marking a fact replaced by newer evidence while keeping the old one and its provenance | Changes: you can answer 'why did the agent believe that in March' | Say: "Overwriting destroys the audit trail we need after an incident."
cards.hook: Append the correction, keep the history

cards.front: Termination reason — why chart it?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent finished | Actually: which of seven mechanisms ended the run — goal condition, step cap, token cap, cost cap, wall-clock, oscillation, error | Changes: rising budget_exhausted becomes your earliest quality alarm | Say: "Distribution first: are we finishing, or giving up inside the cap?"
cards.hook: Weeks of warning before a ticket

cards.front: Test-time compute / inference-time scaling — what is the claim?
cards.back: Sold as: models get smarter if you let them think longer | Actually: more inference compute per query — longer chains, sampling then selecting; SWE-bench went 4.4% to 71.7% in a year | Changes: reasoning depth becomes a per-request budget, and past a point accuracy drops | Say: "Latency is the binding constraint, not cost. Which queries earn depth?"
cards.hook: Overthinking is a measured failure mode
cards.aryaka: Interactive ticket replies stay shallow; overnight RCA drafting can afford depth.

cards.front: The three loops — name them and their timescales.
cards.back: Sold as: one agent loop | Actually: inner (agent, seconds), middle (harness/session, minutes), outer (LLMOps, weeks) | Changes: which loop owns a fix — retry, compaction, or an eval-set entry and a deploy | Say: "That's an outer-loop fix; the inner loop can't learn it."
cards.hook: Seconds, minutes, weeks — three owners

cards.front: Tool contract — what does a tool declare?
cards.back: Sold as: connect the agent to our APIs | Actually: name, typed arguments, semantics, error shape, side-effect class and idempotency — a governed interface, versioned like an API | Changes: tool changes need deprecation windows because prompts and evals depend on them | Say: "A schema change is a breaking change for every agent and eval downstream."
cards.hook: Tools are API contracts, not helpers
cards.aryaka: MyAryaka read tools versus change-execution tools need different side-effect classes.

cards.front: Trajectory evaluation — what does it catch that task success misses?
cards.back: Sold as: measure if the agent is right | Actually: scoring the path — correct trajectories over total — catching right answers reached by wrong, repeated or skipped steps | Changes: you find the agent that is lucky rather than correct | Say: "Task success hides route quality; trajectory success exposes it."
cards.hook: Right answer, wrong route

cards.front: Vibe coding — what did the Replit incident actually demonstrate?
cards.back: Sold as: let the agent build it, review later | Actually: an agent with production credentials and no gate deleted a live database during a publicized experiment | Changes: the lesson is blast radius and side-effect class, not model quality | Say: "It wasn't a bad model. It was an ungated write to production."
cards.hook: The credential, not the vibe

cards.front: Working memory — why is calling it a store wrong?
cards.back: Sold as: the agent's RAM | Actually: the assembled context for one step — a build artifact produced by an assembly function | Changes: you ask what put a fact there, not what is in there | Say: "Nothing is in working memory. Things get put there, every step."
cards.hook: A build artifact, not a store

cards.front: World models — what is being claimed?
cards.back: Sold as: AI that understands physical reality | Actually: a learned latent simulator (JEPA) rolled forward under candidate actions, scored by a cost module, executed by an MPC planner | Changes: nothing on our roadmap — our environment is APIs with side effects, and benchmarks find current models brittle | Say: "Frontier, not roadmap. Placing it precisely is the signal."
cards.hook: $1.03B seed, zero enterprise use today

cards.front: Three-tier cascade at 70/25/5 — say the blended cost out loud.
cards.back: 0.70 × $0.10 + 0.25 × $3.00 + 0.05 × $15.00 = $1.57 per million tokens, against $15.00 for top-tier-only. That is 9.6x cheaper for about one extra second on 30% of queries.
cards.hook: Nine-point-six times, for one second on a third of traffic.

cards.front: Why is a 0.95 tier-1 confidence threshold a mistake?
cards.back: Almost nothing escalates — yet tier 1 is wrong about 5% of the time on exactly those queries. Set tier 1 at 0.85, accept 15% wrong there, and escalate the rest.
cards.hook: A threshold so high it disables the cascade.

cards.front: Three chargeback models for AI usage, and the 2026 default.
cards.back: Bundled — AI is in the subscription and you eat the cost. Metered — pass cost through plus margin. Tiered — free to N queries, then metered. Most SaaS in 2026 is moving to tiered.
cards.hook: Tiered captures heavy users without alienating light ones.

cards.front: The two cost-anomaly thresholds and what each one does.
cards.back: Cost above 2x baseline pages on-call; above 5x auto-degrades. Cost is a leading indicator of loop explosions, tenant load tests and retry storms — treat it with the seriousness of error rate.
cards.hook: In AI, cost IS a reliability signal.

cards.front: What is cache-aware routing?
cards.back: Routing a request to the replica that already holds its prefix in cache rather than round-robin. Round-robin throws away the hit you already paid for.
cards.hook: Round-robin discards your cache

cards.front: Why do long conversations get both slower and more expensive?
cards.back: The KV cache grows with context, so each new token attends over more state — memory and time per token rise with conversation length, not just total tokens billed.
cards.hook: Cost and latency both scale with length

cards.front: Prefill versus decode — why does the distinction matter?
cards.back: Prefill processes input in parallel; decode generates one token at a time. It is the model everything hangs off — big prompts hurt TTFT, big outputs hurt throughput.
cards.hook: One parallel phase, one sequential

cards.front: The classic prompt-caching own-goal.
cards.back: Editing the stable prefix, which invalidates the cache for every consumer at once. A one-word system-prompt tweak can multiply the bill.
cards.hook: One word, whole cache gone

cards.front: What must the prompt layout obey to earn caching?
cards.back: Stable prefix first — system prompt and tool definitions — variable content last. The provider caches a prefix, so ordering is a cost decision.
cards.hook: Prefix order is a cost decision

cards.front: The five token-reduction techniques, in priority order.
cards.back: System-prompt compaction by hoisting tool defs to MCP, 15-25%. Conversation summarization past turn 6, 10-20%. Tool-result truncation with a citation link, 10-15%. Few-shot curation to three, 5-10%. JSON schema output, 5-10%.
cards.hook: No new infra, no model swap — just payload engineering.

cards.front: RAG works at 10K docs and fails at 100M. What actually changed?
cards.back: It became a distributed systems problem: sharding, cross-shard merge and global rerank, coordination overhead and tail latency, incremental indexing instead of full reindexing.
cards.hook: A single index stops being practical

cards.front: "Why do more models make a system stronger?" What is being tested?
cards.back: Allocation of intelligence, not model strength. Small models take intent detection, routing, classification, extraction, validation, guardrails; large models take complex reasoning, planning, final synthesis.
cards.hook: Allocate intelligence intelligently

cards.front: Multiple teams want LLM access. What is the answer, and its cost?
cards.back: One central gateway: auth, per-team quotas, rate limits, routing, prompt templates, logging, cost attribution, retries, fallbacks, policy checks. Cost is platform complexity; gain is governance and one stable API.
cards.hook: Integrate once, swap behind it

cards.front: Why is embedding search alone insufficient in production RAG?
cards.back: Error codes, API names, function names, config keys and product IDs are exact-match problems. BM25 over an inverted index catches what embeddings blur; merge then rerank.
cards.hook: "error 429" is not a semantic query
cards.aryaka: Device models, error codes and CLI strings in our runbooks are exactly this class.

cards.front: Recall or precision in RAG — which do you optimize?
cards.back: High recall first, then reranking for precision before context reaches the model. Missing the document is catastrophic; flooding the window with noise costs answers, latency and money.
cards.hook: Recall first, precision by rerank

cards.front: Four moves that hold a 10M-doc RAG under two seconds.
cards.back: Metadata filters before retrieval, ANN instead of exact nearest-neighbour, reranking bounded to a small candidate set, and caching for repeated queries and hot embeddings.
cards.hook: Filter before you search

cards.front: Why is cost per task the wrong Tier 1 number on its own?
cards.back: Cost per task times error rate gives cost per correct task. AI that is 50% cheaper but 20% less accurate can be more expensive per correct outcome. Always quality-adjust before reporting.
cards.hook: Cheaper per attempt, dearer per outcome.

cards.front: The three layers of cost attribution, and which to ship first.
cards.back: Layer 1 request tags — tenant, feature, user, request. Layer 2 trace aggregation across a trace's 3-10 calls. Layer 3 tenant rollup to the warehouse. Ship 1 and 2 before scaling; chargeback is v2.
cards.hook: Scaling without visibility hits $30K before anyone notices.
cards.aryaka: Tags plus trace aggregation are the precondition for taking the copilot past pilot.

cards.front: Token discipline versus model swapping — which one pays?
cards.back: Token discipline took a copilot from $0.42 to $0.18 per ticket, 57%, with no model change and no quality loss. The model swap would have saved $0.04 and cost 8-12% quality.
cards.hook: Five times the ROI, and no quality tax.
cards.aryaka: At 1,000 tickets/day that gap is $87K/year for about three sprints of prompt work.

cards.front: An LLM call arrives with no tenant or feature tag. Do what?
cards.back: Refuse it. Tags are injected by a thin wrapper from request-scoped context, so engineers cannot bypass them — they call your wrapper, not the SDK. Audit at code review.
cards.hook: Non-negotiable: no tag, no call.

cards.front: How does the AI testing pyramid invert the traditional one?
cards.back: Prompt unit tests are the smallest investment; the 50-200 example regression eval set is the largest. Quality is emergent from prompt plus model plus tools, not from any component.
cards.hook: Eval set at the base, unit tests at the tip

cards.front: Approval bypass rate — exact numerator and denominator.
cards.back: Actions taken without required approval / actions requiring approval. Target 0%. It is the cheapest deterministic gate for an agent that acts.
cards.hook: One bypass in a quarter is still a fail

cards.front: The funnel that keeps an agent team honest about value.
cards.back: Signal generated, reviewed, accepted, acted on, customer contacted, intervention, business outcome, ARR protected. Stops the team optimizing only technical metrics.
cards.hook: 95% accuracy, 10% action rate
cards.aryaka: For a CSM-facing health agent, action rate is the metric that maps to retained ARR.

cards.front: The canary rule that catches what pre-launch eval cannot.
cards.back: Ship to 5% of traffic for 48 hours; auto-rollback if CSAT drops more than 0.3 points below baseline. Hard rule, no overrides.
cards.hook: 0.3 points, 48 hours, no overrides

cards.front: Why is cost per successful task better than token cost?
cards.back: Total evaluation cost / successful tasks. Failed runs burn tokens too, so they inflate the numerator without earning a denominator — raw token cost hides that.
cards.hook: Failures count in the numerator only

cards.front: Name the things an LLM judge must never score.
cards.back: Exact values, classifications, tool names, tool arguments, state transitions, policy rules, approval requirements, API success or failure, latency, token count, cost, call counts.
cards.hook: assert expected_tool == actual_tool

cards.front: How do you report an eval result honestly?
cards.back: Bootstrap the interval — resample results 10,000 times — and report "84% ± 5", never the bare point estimate. Ten lines of code that permanently change how the team talks about results.
cards.hook: "84%" alone is not honest

cards.front: Eval set of 100, baseline 82%, new prompt 85%. Did it improve?
cards.back: You have learned essentially nothing. The 95% CI on a proportion at n=100, p≈0.83 is roughly ±7.4 points — the intervals overlap enormously.
cards.hook: ±7.4 points swallows a 3-point win

cards.front: Before promising to detect a 2-point improvement, what must you know?
cards.back: Your required eval-set size. Detecting 2 points reliably needs substantially more than 100 cases — power-analyze first rather than promising sensitivity you do not have.
cards.hook: Promise only what n supports

cards.front: Why run the same eval several times at nonzero temperature?
cards.back: Self-consistency across runs is itself a quality metric. A system whose score swings 6 points between identical runs has a stability problem worth knowing about.
cards.hook: Swing between identical runs

cards.front: The single change that most increases eval statistical power.
cards.back: Paired comparison: run both variants on the same cases and analyze differences. It removes case-difficulty variance, so 100 paired cases can detect a real 3-point shift an unpaired test cannot.
cards.hook: Test "did case X improve", not 85>82

cards.front: The line that lands hardest on eval discipline.
cards.back: "Most teams are making ship decisions on differences well inside their noise floor — a random walk they call iteration."
cards.hook: A random walk called iteration

cards.front: "I set temperature to 0 so it's reproducible." What is wrong?
cards.back: Batching effects, floating-point non-associativity across GPU kernel scheduling, and MoE expert routing all add run-to-run variance at temperature 0. Reproducibility comes from pinning the model version and accepting a variance band.
cards.hook: Temperature 0 is not determinism

cards.front: The five classes every agent eval dataset needs.
cards.back: Normal, edge (missing, partial, conflicting), failure (timeout, 500, malformed, rate limit, auth), adversarial (injection, cross-account, conflicting instructions), and real historical cases.
cards.hook: Happy path is one of five classes

cards.front: Why are engineer-written eval sets "wishful thinking"?
cards.back: They come from ticket categories, not real samples. Fix: stratified random sample of 20-50 production items weekly, hand-labelled, with examples rotating out after 90 days.
cards.hook: Categories are not samples

cards.front: The central principle of agentic evaluation, in one line.
cards.back: Evaluate the agent, not just the model. Lower-layer quality never guarantees upper-layer quality: answers can be excellent while the agent picks the wrong tool, skips approval or loops.
cards.hook: Great model, unsafe agent

cards.front: The production default mix of evaluator types.
cards.back: About 70% LLM-as-judge, 20% Python function, 10% exact match, plus human review on a 5-example random sample weekly. Judge cost is roughly $0.05 per example.
cards.hook: 70/20/10 plus five humans a week

cards.front: The four evaluation modes, and what distinguishes them.
cards.back: Replay (historical request plus historical tool responses), offline (frozen fixtures), shadow (live traffic, no actions), live (real actions). Mode decides whether the agent can affect the real world.
cards.hook: Only live touches production state

cards.front: Grounded claim rate — formula and why it beats answer-level scoring.
cards.back: Supported claims / total claims × 100, target >95%. Breaking an answer into claims is more useful than labelling the whole answer grounded or not.
cards.hook: Score the claims, not the answer

cards.front: 95% eval pass rate at VendorCo — what happened after shipping?
cards.back: All 200 eval examples were happy-path. CSAT on AI-handled tickets fell to 3.2 from a 4.5 baseline within two days; the team rolled back by Friday.
cards.hook: Tuesday ship, Friday rollback

cards.front: What must humans, not judges, score — and on what scale?
cards.back: Accuracy, actionability, clarity, completeness, trust, each 1-5, target above 4. Humans own business usefulness, trust, UX quality and strategic recommendations.
cards.hook: No judge can score actionability

cards.front: Four ways LLM-as-a-judge misleads you.
cards.back: It misunderstands the reference, favors verbose answers, exhibits model bias, and disagrees with deterministic business rules. Never make it the only evaluation mechanism.
cards.hook: Longer answer, higher score

cards.front: What do you do with an example the judge scores inconsistently?
cards.back: Send it to human review. Judge disagreement with itself across 3 runs is a judge-variance signal, and those examples are exactly where ground truth is needed.
cards.hook: Ask the judge three times

cards.front: The A/B rule for swapping the model behind an agent.
cards.back: Two weeks at 90% old / 10% new, measuring CSAT, resolution rate, escalation rate, cost per ticket. Roll to 50% after 7 flat-or-better days; roll back on any metric down over 5%.
cards.hook: Eval says better, users often disagree

cards.front: Why is "Agent Score = 87%" a dangerous number?
cards.back: It blends dimensions that are not comparable: a 1% safety violation rate on critical actions is not equivalent to 1% less answer quality.
cards.hook: 87% is where safety failures hide

cards.front: What does online eval sampling look like in production?
cards.back: Run an LLM judge over 5% of live traffic scoring helpfulness, accuracy and tone; track the distribution daily and alert on distribution shift.
cards.hook: 5% scored online beats 100% pre-launch

cards.front: Policy violation rate — formula, and the threshold trap.
cards.back: Policy violations / total test cases × 100. Target 0% for critical actions. Do not treat safety like accuracy, where 95% is acceptable.
cards.hook: 95% passes accuracy, fails safety

cards.front: The conjunction that declares an agent production-ready.
cards.back: Safety violations = 0 AND policy bypasses = 0 AND task success >95% AND groundedness >95%. A multidimensional scorecard with hard gates, never a weighted average.
cards.hook: AND, never a weighted average

cards.front: What runs against production immediately after every deploy?
cards.back: 5-10 real requests: response inside 30s, no trace error, expected shape, one LLM-judge "is this reasonable?" check. Any failure triggers auto-rollback.
cards.hook: Ten real requests or you are flying blind

cards.front: The single shape shared by every investigated 2025-2026 AI failure.
cards.back: A team optimized a proxy — pass rate, latency, cost — and it diverged from the real metric. The fix is measuring the real metric online, not picking a better proxy.
cards.hook: Never pick a better proxy

cards.front: Recovery success rate — formula, target, and what it demands of you.
cards.back: Recovered failures / total failure scenarios × 100, target >90%. Requires injecting timeouts, HTTP 500s, malformed data, empty results, unauthorized and rate-limit responses.
cards.hook: You must break the tools to measure it

cards.front: The evaluation flywheel, in order.
cards.back: Production, real agent traces, failures and edge cases, curated eval cases, regression suite, agent improvement, back to production. Worth more than one static benchmark.
cards.hook: Every incident buys you a test case

cards.front: How do you test whether an agent's decisions are repeatable?
cards.back: Run one scenario 100 times: 94 correct, 4 partial, 2 failed = 94%. A good agent must not flip HIGH RISK to LOW RISK on identical evidence.
cards.hook: Same evidence twice, same verdict

cards.front: Retrieval precision — formula and the worked example.
cards.back: Relevant retrieved / total retrieved. Retrieved D1, D5, D20, D25 with only D1 and D5 relevant gives 2/4 = 50%. Answers: how much noise did we pull?
cards.hook: Precision's denominator is what you pulled

cards.front: Retrieval recall — formula and the worked example.
cards.back: Relevant retrieved / total relevant. Relevant D1, D5, D9; retrieved D1, D5 gives 2/3 = 66.7%. Answers: did we fetch what the answer needed?
cards.hook: Recall's denominator is what exists

cards.front: What does shadow evaluation give you that offline cannot?
cards.back: Realistic production traffic through the new agent with no real actions and no user impact — the way to validate a new model, prompt or policy before it can hurt anyone.
cards.hook: Real traffic, zero consequences

cards.front: State transition correctness — formula and target.
cards.back: Valid transitions / total transitions × 100, target 100%. DETECTED to ANALYZING to APPROVAL_PENDING to APPROVED to ACTIONED is valid; DETECTED to ACTIONED is not.
cards.hook: DETECTED to ACTIONED skips the approval

cards.front: How do you stratify an eval set, and in what proportions?
cards.back: Simple 40%, medium 30%, hard 20%, adversarial 10%; report pass rate per stratum. A 95% aggregate is consistent with 30% failure on realistic traffic.
cards.hook: Aggregate pass rate averages away the hard cases

cards.front: Task success rate — formula and what it cannot see.
cards.back: Successful tasks / total tasks × 100. 92 of 100 cases complete = 92%. A primary top-level metric that says nothing about the path taken.
cards.hook: Top line that hides a 23-step trajectory

cards.front: Which eval metric catches a perfectly working tool doing damage?
cards.back: Tool argument accuracy, target >99%. Expected account_id A123, agent sent A132. The tool works flawlessly on the wrong customer.
cards.hook: Two transposed digits, wrong customer's data
cards.aryaka: In a multi-tenant SASE stack a wrong account_id is a cross-tenant read, not a typo.

cards.front: Tool-call success rate was 100%. What did it miss for three weeks?
cards.back: 47 calls went to upgrade_ticket instead of update_ticket; every call "succeeded." Monitor tool-call distribution weekly, not just success rate. Damage: about $30K.
cards.hook: 100% success, 47 wrong tools

cards.front: Tool call efficiency — formula and the caveat.
cards.back: Optimal tool calls / actual tool calls. 5 optimal, 10 actual = 50%. Use as a diagnostic metric, never as a universal quality score.
cards.hook: 50% efficiency is not 50% quality

cards.front: send_email() returned FAILED. What is the agent's hallucination called?
cards.back: Tool hallucination — the agent claims a tool returned information it did not. It reports "Email has been sent." Track it apart from answer quality.
cards.hook: The tool failed; the agent reported success

cards.front: Tool selection accuracy — formula and target.
cards.back: Correct tool selections / total tool selections × 100; scorecard target >98%. Asked for traffic data, the agent called get_customer_profile — that is a failure.
cards.hook: get_traffic wanted, get_customer_profile called

cards.front: Trajectory success rate — formula and what it catches.
cards.back: Correct trajectories / total trajectories × 100. Catches the agent that reached a correct answer through wrong, repeated or skipped steps — invisible to task success rate.
cards.hook: Right answer, wrong route

cards.front: Why is final-answer correctness insufficient for an agent?
cards.back: Agent A: 5 steps, 3 tool calls, 8s. Agent B: 23 steps, 17 calls, 45s. Both report 100% task success; B is operationally broken.
cards.hook: Two agents, one score, 5x the latency

cards.front: Evidence says traffic declined 32%. What makes the answer ungrounded?
cards.back: The agent adds "and the customer is considering leaving Aryaka." Claim one is supported; claim two was invented. Groundedness is poor even though it reads well.
cards.hook: One real number, one invented intention

cards.front: An unusual ticket at 2:14 AM sent the agent into a reflection loop.
cards.back: ❌ Tool A, B, C all failed, so it reflected and retried for four hours — $40,200, no cap, no alarm. ✅ Step cap, cost cap, wall-clock cap and oscillation detection on hashed (tool, args).
cards.hook: $40K bought by five defensible decisions

cards.front: A planner-executor agent with six tools, no budget object.
cards.back: ❌ $47K in six hours — from 'everything is fine' to the CFO asking about reversing charges. ✅ A typed budget nested into every sub-agent, plus per-tenant daily cost ceilings.
cards.hook: Six hours, start to CFO

cards.front: A chatbot promised a bereavement-fare policy that did not exist.
cards.back: ❌ The 'chatbot is a separate legal entity' defense was rejected; the airline was held liable. ✅ One source of truth, citation-or-abstain, and no policy claims without a retrieved source.
cards.hook: Your agent's promises are your promises

cards.front: 'Agent wants to act — Approve?' on every action.
cards.back: ❌ 99% approval rate: a control that controls nothing, plus a latency tax. ✅ Show the concrete artifact, and auto-approve inside deterministic bounds.
cards.hook: A gate everyone waves through is a tax

cards.front: `while True` with the model deciding when to stop.
cards.back: ❌ Autonomy theater — unbounded cost and latency, undebuggable. ✅ A state machine with hard caps on steps, tokens, cost and wall-clock.
cards.hook: The model is not a scheduler

cards.front: The engineer who built it also wrote the eval set.
cards.back: ❌ Same mental model as the bug — blind to exactly the failures that matter. ✅ A domain expert authors the adversarial set.
cards.hook: You cannot grade your own blind spot
cards.aryaka: Tier-1 engineers should write the NOC eval set, not the automation team.

cards.front: Everything the agent has ever seen, in every prompt.
cards.back: ❌ Cost up, latency up, accuracy down — context rot with no error raised. ✅ A per-step context assembly function that decides what enters the window.
cards.hook: Accumulation is a design choice, badly made

cards.front: No state object — the message history is the record.
cards.back: ❌ No resumability, no idempotency, duplicate actions on retry. ✅ A typed, persisted state object checkpointed per step.
cards.hook: History is a log, not a database

cards.front: All customers embedded into one shared vector index.
cards.back: ❌ Customer A's query returned Customer B's contract clause; contract voided, feature killed, CISO fired. ✅ Per-tenant namespaces plus a tenant_id filter enforced below the query API.
cards.hook: Similarity has no concept of tenancy
cards.aryaka: One index per customer namespace — a SASE provider cannot survive one cross-tenant answer.

cards.front: Grading only the final response.
cards.back: ❌ Misses wrong-policy-right-prose: fluent answers reached through wrong steps. ✅ Trace-level evals scoring the trajectory, not just the output.
cards.hook: Right answer, wrong route, invisible

cards.front: The framework's default flow becomes the design.
cards.back: ❌ You inherit someone else's trade-offs and can't explain your own. ✅ Design the flow first, then pick a framework to implement it.
cards.hook: LangGraph is an implementation, not a decision

cards.front: One prompt doing classification, retrieval, policy, tool choice and writing.
cards.back: ❌ A 3,000-token God Prompt — untestable, unlocalizable, brittle. ✅ Decompose into contracted steps, each independently evaluable.
cards.hook: You cannot unit-test a paragraph

cards.front: A copilot with $2,500 refund authority invented a 30-day policy.
cards.back: ❌ It issued $1,200, the screenshot went viral, and the settlement was $480K. The corpus was the disease. ✅ Corpus hygiene plus a hard rule: no policy statement without a cited retrieved source.
cards.hook: The hallucination was the symptom

cards.front: 200 eval examples, all clear-intent single-step happy path, 95% pass.
cards.back: ❌ Production tickets were ambiguous, multi-intent and angry; CSAT fell 4.5 to 3.2 in two days. ✅ Sample the eval set from real production traffic, including the frustrated and malformed tail.
cards.hook: 95% on the wrong distribution

cards.front: Only the happy path is designed.
cards.back: ❌ The tail is where users churn and incidents live — 95% eval pass, tanked CSAT. ✅ Design the handoff and out-of-scope paths as first-class flows.
cards.hook: The tail is the product

cards.front: Every team integrating the model provider directly.
cards.back: ❌ No quotas, no cost attribution, no failover, N integrations to change. ✅ One gateway; teams integrate once and the platform swaps providers behind it.
cards.hook: N integrations, N migrations

cards.front: Blaming a wrong answer on hallucination.
cards.back: ❌ "The model hallucinated" — no stage, no owner, no fix. ✅ Check top-K for the source passage: absent is retrieval, present is generation.
cards.hook: Structure beats a label

cards.front: Sending every request to the strongest model.
cards.back: ❌ A simple FAQ answered by the biggest model — wasteful by default. ✅ Small models classify and route; escalate only when complexity demands it.
cards.hook: Expensive intelligence, trivial task

cards.front: Defending injection with prompt separation alone.
cards.back: ❌ Security that depends on the model behaving correctly. ✅ Retrieved content triggers no actions; every tool call validated server-side; least privilege; approval on sensitive actions.
cards.hook: Real security lives outside the prompt

cards.front: Restarting a workflow that failed at step 8.
cards.back: ❌ Replays seven successful steps, including their side effects. ✅ Persist state and checkpoints; resume from the last successful step.
cards.hook: Resumability, not repetition

cards.front: Text logs from a 40-step agent run.
cards.back: ❌ No causal structure, so failures can't be localized to a step. ✅ Structured tracing with a step hierarchy and one correlation id.
cards.hook: grep cannot reconstruct causality

cards.front: Five agents because that's the architecture.
cards.back: ❌ Cost, latency and debugging pain with no measured benefit. ✅ Collapse to a pipeline; keep LLMs only where judgment is genuinely needed.
cards.hook: An org chart is not an architecture

cards.front: Provider outage takes the product down.
cards.back: ❌ A single point of failure you don't own or control. ✅ Fallback model, cached path, human handoff — a defined degradation ladder.
cards.hook: Design the bad day, not just the good one

cards.front: The agent runs as admin or a shared service account.
cards.back: ❌ Blast radius equals everything the account can reach. ✅ Per-tool least privilege with short-lived tokens.
cards.hook: One credential, one incident
cards.aryaka: A read-only MyAryaka token and a separate gated change token, never one service account.

cards.front: Business rules written into the system prompt.
cards.back: ❌ Prompt-as-policy — a suggestion, not a guarantee, and injectable. ✅ Rules in code, enforced before execution, not requested in text.
cards.hook: Prompts persuade; code enforces
cards.aryaka: Refund and config-change limits belong in the tool wrapper, not the prompt.

cards.front: 'We'll add auth and tenancy before GA.'
cards.back: ❌ GA arrives; the work doesn't. Retrofitting isolation means rewriting retrieval. ✅ Tenancy and authz land before the first write path ships.
cards.hook: Security debt compounds at GA speed

cards.front: Tool 500s trigger retry-3x, then restart the loop with a 'try differently' prefix.
cards.back: ❌ Each restart grew the context, so cost per attempt climbed while the loop never converged. ✅ Circuit-break the failing tool and fail the run; never restart with accumulated context.
cards.hook: Retries multiply; they don't converge

cards.front: Fifty-turn conversations quietly exceeded the 200K window.
cards.back: ❌ The provider truncated the oldest turns silently — no error, just an agent that forgot the ticket's origin. ✅ Count tokens yourself, compact on a threshold, and alert on compaction rate.
cards.hook: The provider fails open, not loud

cards.front: Prompts, models and corpus changing untracked.
cards.back: ❌ 'It got worse and we don't know why' — with no way to bisect. ✅ Version everything and stamp the versions into every trace.
cards.hook: Untraceable change is unfixable regression

cards.front: update_ticket and upgrade_ticket both registered, both well-built.
cards.back: ❌ 47 wrong calls over three weeks — real plan upgrades, customer emails, zero alerts. ✅ Distinct names, side-effect classes, and a confirmation gate on anything customer-visible.
cards.hook: No spike, no complaint, three weeks
cards.aryaka: 'update_ticket' vs 'escalate_ticket' vs 'apply_config' need different gates, not similar schemas.

cards.front: Event-driven cache invalidation that was sound in design.
cards.back: ❌ A KB update fired no invalidation for semantically-near entries; deprecated config guidance kept serving. ✅ Version the corpus, key cache entries by that version, and expire on version bump — not on events.
cards.hook: Sound design, unimplemented invalidation
cards.aryaka: A stale MTU or threshold answer is a black-holed site, not a saved dollar.

cards.front: Executing on a user_id or amount the model produced.
cards.back: ❌ Authorization bypass — the model becomes the source of identity. ✅ Re-derive identity and limits server-side, then verify before execution.
cards.hook: Model output is a request, not a claim

cards.front: Everything remembered forever.
cards.back: ❌ Stale contradictions surfacing months later, plus compliance liability. ✅ TTLs, provenance on every fact, and working deletion paths.
cards.hook: Memory without deletion is liability

cards.front: Structured facts stored as embeddings.
cards.back: ❌ Probabilistic answers to deterministic questions — 'which tier is ACME on' returned by similarity. ✅ Storage by access pattern: relational for facts, vectors for meaning.
cards.hook: Never ask a vector for an exact fact

cards.front: A customer PDF carried white-on-white font-size-1 instructions.
cards.back: ❌ Retrieval embedded it; any later ticket that retrieved the chunk exfiltrated PII via the CRM tool. ✅ Treat retrieved text as untrusted, strip invisible content at ingestion, and gate egress tools.
cards.hook: The corpus became the attack surface
cards.aryaka: Customer-uploaded configs and diagrams are exactly this vector for us.

cards.front: Shipping on 'it seems better than last week'.
cards.back: ❌ Silent regressions with no way to compare versions. ✅ An eval suite in CI, gating the deploy.
cards.hook: No baseline, no regression, no idea

cards.front: Your approval rate is above 95%. What is that?
cards.back: Approval theater, not a control. The response is to shrink what needs a human with deterministic auto-approve bands, and make the remainder genuinely informative.
cards.hook: A gate everyone waves through is a latency tax.

cards.front: What must approval do architecturally, and operationally?
cards.back: Suspend and persist, never block a thread — that's what makes hours-long waits survivable. Then notification on suspend, a visible pending queue, a TTL, and time-to-decide as a metric.
cards.hook: Any approval without a timeout accumulates orphaned workflows.

cards.front: budget_exhausted share is climbing. What is it telling you?
cards.back: The agent is giving up, not finishing — the earliest and clearest signal of quality decay. It usually precedes user complaints by weeks. Alert on it.
cards.hook: Weeks of warning before anyone files a ticket.

cards.front: What must exhausted() return, and why?
cards.back: Which cap fired, logged to the trace. "Ran out of budget" is unactionable; "ran out of steps having spent 12% of the cost budget" says the step cap is miscalibrated.
cards.hook: Teams pick 10 as a round number and never learn.

cards.front: Why never put "you have used 6 of 10 tool calls" in the prompt?
cards.back: The model can't count reliably and can be argued out of a constraint. Budgets, permissions, and termination caps are harness state, enforced in code.
cards.hook: The harness owns budgets; the model owns judgment.

cards.front: Two caveats that show you've operated compaction.
cards.back: The raw transcript always goes to the trace — compaction is never data deletion. And compaction is a model call that can hallucinate, so eval it against ground truth.
cards.hook: Its errors are durable within the run and invisible afterwards.

cards.front: What is the signature post-compaction failure?
cards.back: The agent re-attempts an approach it already ruled out, because the reasoning that ruled it out was summarized away. Preserve a tried-and-rejected list explicitly.
cards.hook: The one row every team drops.

cards.front: When and into what should you compact?
cards.back: Trigger at 60–70% of the window, not the limit — compaction needs headroom. Compact into a schema: goal, constraints, decisions, findings, tried_and_failed, current_state, open. Keep the last N turns verbatim.
cards.hook: Hitting the ceiling mid-compaction is a hard failure.

cards.front: Why must consolidation distil only from primary sources?
cards.back: Distil from user statements and tool results, never prior model output. Otherwise a hallucinated fact gets re-consolidated from responses containing it and reinforced instead of corrected.
cards.hook: A slow-motion data-corruption loop.

cards.front: Which consolidation summarizer is better: 70%/99% or 95%/90%?
cards.back: 70% of facts at 99% precision. Consolidation errors are durable and self-reinforcing, so precision is weighted far above recall and gets its own eval suite.
cards.hook: Recall costs you a gap; precision failures corrupt the store.

cards.front: A user deletes a conversation. What still exists?
cards.back: The consolidated summary distilled from it, that summary's embedding, the trace, caches, backups, and eval datasets. Deletion must propagate across all of them.
cards.hook: Retrofit provenance later and your only honest option is deleting everything derived.

cards.front: What does deterministic replay give you?
cards.back: Record every model response in the trace, then replay the harness against them: reproducible debugging, zero-token regression tests, and "would the new policy have handled last week's incident?"
cards.hook: Turns your trace store into a test corpus.

cards.front: What is error amplification in a loop, and the fix?
cards.back: Raw errors accumulate in context, the model pattern-matches on failure, quality decays. Normalize errors to {error_code, retryable, what_to_try_instead}, keep the latest per tool, cap 2–3 consecutive.
cards.hook: Two failures in context and the run is already worse.

cards.front: Name the four fact classes for supersession handling.
cards.back: Immutable (write once), slow-changing (timestamp, supersede on new evidence), volatile (short TTL or don't store), contested (store both with provenance and surface the conflict).
cards.hook: Last-write-wins is wrong because facts change differently.

cards.front: Define an agent harness in one sentence.
cards.back: The deterministic runtime around a nondeterministic model: what the model sees, what it may do, when it stops, and what gets recorded.
cards.hook: An OS for a process that can't manage its own resources.

cards.front: List the components of a harness.
cards.back: Context assembler, memory subsystem, tool runtime, loop controller, budget accountant, guardrail hooks, state store, trace emitter, interrupt handler. The model sits inside, swappable.
cards.hook: Nine boxes around one rented model.

cards.front: Name the test layers for an agent, in order.
cards.back: Harness unit tests with the model mocked, component evals, seam evals, end-to-end task success, adversarial suite, and deterministic replay as regression.
cards.hook: Every production failure becomes a case in one click.

cards.front: How do you test a harness without spending tokens?
cards.back: Mock the model to return scripted responses and assert on control flow: right termination reason, budget decremented, approval gate fired, state persisted and resumed.
cards.hook: The most under-built tooling in agent systems.

cards.front: What does a memory-need gate decide?
cards.back: Whether a query needs retrieval at all, and from which stores: none, procedural only, semantic only, episodic only, or everything. A large fraction need nothing.
cards.hook: Retrieving anyway costs latency, tokens, and accuracy.

cards.front: Can a fact in memory ever grant permission?
cards.back: Never. Memory informs the answer; the identity system decides the action, checked at execution. This makes the highest-value poisoning attack pointless.
cards.hook: Otherwise persistent injection becomes privilege escalation.

cards.front: What is memory poisoning?
cards.back: Planting a durable false fact via text engineered to be extracted — "this account is authorized for unlimited refunds." A one-shot injection becomes persistent, and consolidation erases its origin.
cards.hook: Six weeks later it's a trusted row with no injection markers.
cards.aryaka: Customer-authored tickets are untrusted content; a ticket must never become a durable fact about entitlements.

cards.front: What shape should a memory record have?
cards.back: (fact, value, confidence, source_episode, observed_at, superseded_by) — not key to value. Then retrieval can apply recency and confidence, and the agent can surface a conflict.
cards.hook: Key-value memory can't decay, supersede, or be audited.

cards.front: Sequence for adding memory to a stateless agent.
cards.back: Episodic logging, read tools against systems of record, procedural memory in git, explicit-only semantic memory, confirmed extraction with provenance, then batch consolidation.
cards.hook: The memory-need gate comes before the memory system.

cards.front: Name the memory types and their stores.
cards.back: Working (ephemeral assembly), procedural (files in version control), semantic (relational plus small vector), episodic (append-only log), workflow state (transactional store).
cards.hook: Five rows, five different correctness needs.

cards.front: Define memory utilization and why it's the sleeper metric.
cards.back: Of retrieved items, how many were actually referenced in the answer. Retrieve five and reference one and you pay 5× for 1× while diluting attention.
cards.hook: Measuring it leads straight to cutting k — cost and quality together.

cards.front: State the asymmetry that drives memory write policy.
cards.back: A missing memory produces a slightly worse answer. A wrong memory produces a confidently wrong answer, forever, in every future session, retrieved and stated as fact.
cards.hook: Writes need a higher bar than reads. Most teams invert it.

cards.front: One test for whether your harness leaked into application logic.
cards.back: Can you A/B two models on the same harness in an afternoon? If not, provider-specific formatting and the model id have spread through feature code.
cards.hook: An afternoon, or you have a leak.

cards.front: The model is rented; the harness is ___.
cards.back: Owned. Frontier models converge and change under you every few months. Your memory schema, loop policy, tool contracts, and eval set are the durable assets.
cards.hook: So the model is the last variable you change, not the first.

cards.front: What is most "memory" in an enterprise agent, actually?
cards.back: Tool calls to systems of record that already own the truth — CRM, warehouse, ticketing. The genuine memory layer is only the residue: soft context and relationship history.
cards.hook: A vector copy of Salesforce facts is the classic wrong turn.

cards.front: How do you detect a doom loop cheaply?
cards.back: Hash (tool_name, normalized_args) per call. Break if a hash repeats three or more times, or if a cycle of length two to three repeats.
cards.hook: Read file, edit, read file, edit the same thing back.

cards.front: 85% per-step reliability over 10 and 20 steps?
cards.back: About 20% end-to-end at 10 steps and ~4% at 20. You cannot buy long-horizon reliability from a better model.
cards.hook: Shorten the chain, verify intermediate states, or add a human checkpoint.

cards.front: Why are per-tool caps separate from the step cap?
cards.back: An agent that may call read_file 30 times should still call send_email once. Caps are per risky tool, and budgets are per-tenant configurable.
cards.hook: Unlimited reads, one draft, zero sends.
cards.aryaka: An enterprise tenant's live incident earns a larger envelope than a free-tier query — configure budgets per tenant.

cards.front: How should procedural memory (skills, playbooks) be governed?
cards.back: As code: version control, code review, versioned per deploy, tested by evals, rolled back like a deploy. Not editable in a console, not auto-updated by the system.
cards.hook: If it changes behaviour, it ships like code.

cards.front: How does progressive disclosure make 200 procedures affordable?
cards.back: Always in context: name plus one-line description, a few dozen tokens each. Loaded on demand: the full body. Loaded if needed: linked references and scripts.
cards.hook: Write descriptions as triggers, not titles, or the skill never fires.

cards.front: Which harness behaviour silently destroys its own prompt cache?
cards.back: Reordering or editing prior messages. The growing transcript is a stable prefix within a run, so caching helps — until the harness rewrites earlier turns.
cards.hook: A subtle and expensive bug.

cards.front: 6-step runs cost $0.08; 7% hit the 40-step cap at $2.40. Blended?
cards.back: 93% × $0.08 = $0.074 plus 7% × $2.40 = $0.168, so $0.242 — 3× the tested estimate, with the tail carrying 69% of the bill.
cards.hook: Your average cost is a lie; budget on p95.

cards.front: Cumulative input tokens for a naive loop at 5, 20, 40 iterations?
cards.back: With a 2k base and ~1.5k tool results: ~28k at 5, ~305k at 20, ~1.14M at 40. Total input is O(N²); iteration 40 alone costs ~30× iteration 1.
cards.hook: The most important economics fact about agent loops.

cards.front: Which facts belong in a table rather than a vector store?
cards.back: Any fact with a schema: customer tier, preferred contact, account manager, device model. Retrieving those by cosine similarity asks a probabilistic system a deterministic question.
cards.hook: Vector-first means you can't answer "what plan is this customer on".
cards.aryaka: Tenant tier, circuit inventory, and maintenance windows are schema'd facts — read them from the system of record, not embeddings.

cards.front: Name the seven ways an agent loop should be able to end.
cards.back: Model declares done, deterministic goal check, budget exhaustion, no-progress detection, error threshold, human interrupt or approval, external cancellation. A production loop needs all seven.
cards.hook: They're not alternatives.

cards.front: The eight-month stale-preference failure: what was missing?
cards.back: An agent kept recommending Slack after the contact left. No observed_at filter, no confidence decay, no entity-change detection, no inspectable provenance, no metric that would surface it.
cards.hook: Every answer looked fine, so nobody blamed the agent.

cards.front: State versus memory: what's the engineering difference?
cards.back: State is transactional and must be exact — "did we already issue the refund?" Memory is best-effort and advisory — "the customer prefers email." Different stores, different guarantees.
cards.hook: Merging them is the most common architectural error.

cards.front: What do you get from delegating to a bounded sub-loop?
cards.back: It burns ~30k tokens internally and returns a ~300-token findings object. The parent gets a 40-step investigation's effect at a 3-step cost; the mess never enters its context.
cards.hook: Multi-agent as context isolation, not an org chart.

cards.front: Four preconditions for sub-agent delegation to work.
cards.back: The sub-task is genuinely independent, the return contract is typed and compact, budgets nest so a child gets a slice of the parent's, and failures return structured partial results.
cards.hook: Draws as a straight line? It's a pipeline you made expensive.

cards.front: First fix for context growth inside a loop.
cards.back: Summarize tool results on ingestion: a 4,000-token API response becomes a ~200-token structured extract. The raw version goes to the trace, not the context.
cards.hook: 20× smaller per observation; the raw copy lives in the trace.

cards.front: What does a healthy termination-reason distribution look like?
cards.back: goal_verified 62%, model_declared_done 18%, budget_exhausted 11%, stalled 5%, error_threshold 3%, human_interrupt 1%. Sample-audit the unverified slice.
cards.hook: Most informative, least instrumented metric in agent systems.

cards.front: Name the three agent loops and their timescales.
cards.back: Inner: agent loop, seconds, owned by the model. Middle: harness/session, minutes to days, owned by your code. Outer: LLMOps, days to weeks, owned by humans and CI.
cards.hook: Seconds, minutes, weeks — three owners, three failure modes.

cards.front: How do you manufacture a verifiable goal condition?
cards.back: Narrow until a cheap check exists. "Draft an email" → must mention all three disclosures. "Triage this alert" → findings object with a cited runbook and confidence.
cards.hook: Agentic coding works because pytest returns an exit code.

cards.front: When can procedural memory safely grow itself?
cards.back: Only with a verifiable goal condition. Voyager's skill library compounded because success was checkable; without a cheap verifier, auto-accumulated skills are auto-accumulated errors.
cards.hook: Same requirement as loop termination — not a coincidence.

cards.front: Why is "working memory" not a store?
cards.back: It is the output of an assembly function — a per-step build artifact. Calling it context RAM invites teams to accumulate forever instead of deciding what goes in.
cards.hook: Nothing is in working memory; things get put there.

cards.front: Name the five memory write policies.
cards.back: Explicit only, heuristic extraction, LLM salience judgment, post-hoc consolidation, confirmed extraction. Salience gives broad coverage and makes every error permanent; confirmed extraction gives best precision.
cards.hook: Start explicit-only; graduate to confirmed extraction.

cards.front: How should the eval set evolve?
cards.back: Cluster real failed production sessions — slow responses, repeated misunderstandings, rephrasing, drop-offs — and feed those patterns back in. Offline eval must track production reality.
cards.hook: Production failures are the eval backlog

cards.front: Eval score is high, users still complain. What is wrong?
cards.back: Metric mismatch — the eval set does not reflect production usage. Clean questions in eval, vague and messy ones in reality; correctness measured, speed and task completion cared about.
cards.hook: A good model score is not a good system

cards.front: Beyond model metrics, which four product metrics matter?
cards.back: Task completion rate, escalation rate, user correction rate, repeat question rate. They answer whether users are succeeding, which model scores cannot.
cards.hook: Are users actually succeeding?

cards.front: Why does default attribution systematically under-credit AI?
cards.back: Last-touch attribution credits whatever happened last, but AI's contribution sits early in the workflow — triage, drafting, retrieval. Traditional ROI assumes linear attribution; AI ROI is multi-causal.
cards.hook: The AI runs the first mile and gets none of the medal.

cards.front: The four latency thresholds users actually feel.
cards.back: 200ms feels instant; 1s feels responsive; 3s feels slow but acceptable; past 5s users assume the system is broken. If P95 exceeds 3s you have a UX problem wearing a technical costume.
cards.hook: Latency is a product feature, not a technical detail.

cards.front: Why a metric tree beats a single North Star.
