cards.back: One North Star leadership reports; leading indicators the team optimizes daily — intent accuracy, retrieval recall, tool-call success, hallucination rate; guardrails that block regressions — P95, cost per resolution, escalation rate.
cards.hook: Report one, optimize four, guard four.

cards.front: Why must you never blend the three ROI tiers?
cards.back: A blended number buries the strategic story under the cost story. Leadership needs all three visible to make investment decisions — cost savings maintain margin, revenue funds expansion.
cards.hook: Blending hides Tier 3 under Tier 1.

cards.front: You measure resolved-without-human-touch. How does it get gamed?
cards.back: The AI takes easy tickets and refuses hard ones. Capability appears to rise while customer value drops. Fix: weight by ticket difficulty, or pair with a coverage metric — percent of volume attempted, not just resolved.
cards.hook: Optimizing the North Star into uselessness.

cards.front: The failure mode of per-resolution AI pricing.
cards.back: Resolution gaming — easy tickets get classified as resolved and hard ones escalate. Mitigate with an audit trail and independently measured CSAT, and define resolution scope with complexity tiers.
cards.hook: Intercom Fin: $0.39 in 2024, $0.99 in 2026.

cards.front: How do you compute an AI feature's price floor?
cards.back: Model cost per task times 1.5-3x for infra, ops, support and profit. A 16K-token ticket costs about $0.072 on Sonnet, so the floor is $0.14 at 2x and $0.22 at 3x. Most products price at 3-5x model cost.
cards.hook: Below the floor you lose money on every ticket.

cards.front: What makes a quality SLO real instead of decorative?
cards.back: An enforced error budget. Blow the 2% hallucination budget and the system must auto-degrade — safer model, narrower autonomy, higher human-review rate. Without enforcement the team normalizes the drift.
cards.hook: SRE error-budget discipline, applied to quality.
cards.aryaka: Copilot v1 targets: hallucination under 3%, resolution over 50%, human-override under 30%.

cards.front: Three ways to attribute a result to the AI.
cards.back: Counterfactual A/B — hold 10% of tickets out for 30 days; most rigorous, politically hardest. Time-decomposition — track triage, research, draft, review separately. Self-reported — agents under-report 30-50%; sanity check only.
cards.hook: Rigor, decomposition, or vibes — pick two.
cards.aryaka: Time-decomposition is the defensible option on Aryaka's tickets — no customer is withheld from AI.

cards.front: How do you state an ROI number to executives?
cards.back: As a range with its method attached: "$480K annual savings, measured via A/B test, 95% confidence interval plus or minus $80K." Honest ranges build trust; point estimates destroy it.
cards.hook: The method is half the number.

cards.front: The three ROI tiers, their horizons, and their measurability.
cards.back: Tier 1 cost savings: 0-6 months, high, dollars. Tier 2 revenue uplift: 6-18 months, medium, needs an A/B test. Tier 3 capability optionality: 12-36 months, low, directional only.
cards.hook: Stop computing a single ROI number.

cards.front: Four things never to report as AI ROI.
cards.back: Model accuracy alone — pair it with adoption. Token cost alone — pair it with task value. Vanity counts of agents deployed or prompts written. And any ROI before 90 days: novelty and selection bias dominate.
cards.hook: Executives see through activity metrics.

cards.front: Where do gateways leak data?
cards.back: The cache key. It must include model, every output-affecting parameter, and the full permission/tenant scope. A prompt-hash key serves Tenant A's answer to Tenant B — and prompts collide more than you would think.
cards.hook: "Summarize this ticket" collides

cards.front: The gateway build-vs-buy landscape, named.
cards.back: LiteLLM for a fast self-hosted start with virtual keys and budgets; Portkey/Helicone/Cloudflare AI Gateway for managed with a data-boundary question; Kong/Apigee if you already run one; Bedrock/Vertex if committed to a cloud.
cards.hook: LiteLLM is the common default

cards.front: What does a mid-stream client disconnect leave behind?
cards.back: Untracked spend and a dangling upstream request you are still paying for. Handling disconnect separates having built a gateway from having described one.
cards.hook: You still pay for the abandoned stream

cards.front: The hidden cost of a gateway everyone forgets.
cards.back: Its own added latency. Eighty milliseconds on every call is a tax on the whole organization, and it compounds through every step of a multi-step agent run.
cards.hook: 80ms × every call × every team

cards.front: The gateway is now a single point of failure. What does that require?
cards.back: Stateless and horizontally scalable, health-checked, deployed with more care than the apps behind it — and a documented client-side bypass path so a gateway outage does not take down every AI feature.
cards.hook: Document the bypass before you need it

cards.front: The hardest part of a gateway: streaming with accounting.
cards.back: Stream to the client with minimal added latency while counting tokens, applying output guards and writing a trace — accumulate in parallel, finalize the trace on stream close.
cards.hook: Cannot buffer, cannot skip accounting

cards.front: A gateway abstracts providers. What is the trap on both sides?
cards.back: Abstracting to a lowest common denominator makes your best model worse; passing everything through is not an abstraction. Normalize the common 90%, expose a provider-specific escape hatch, version the gateway API.
cards.hook: Normalize 90%, escape-hatch the rest

cards.front: Upstream fails after 300 tokens already streamed. Now what?
cards.back: You cannot transparently retry. Either retry only pre-first-token (clean, limited) or support client-side resumption (complex). Pick one and document it, or clients treat a truncated response as complete.
cards.hook: Truncated reads as complete

cards.front: Why is semantic caching a correctness hazard, not a cost feature?
cards.back: A false hit is a wrong answer served with full confidence, silently. If you do it: tight threshold, tenant-scoped, exclude temporal or personalized content, log every hit with its score, sample-audit.
cards.hook: Mature teams narrow it to FAQ shapes

cards.front: How do teams DoS themselves through a provider?
cards.back: Provider rate limits are per-organization. Team A's batch backfill exhausts the quota and Team B's customer-facing product throws 429s. Solve it at the gateway: per-consumer fair-share quotas, priority classes, a queue for low-priority work.
cards.hook: Your batch job is their outage
cards.aryaka: An overnight re-triage backfill can 429 the live portal copilot unless interactive traffic outranks it.

cards.front: Why does training parallelize while inference cannot?
cards.back: Inference is autoregressive: token 20 cannot exist before token 1. In training the full sequence is known, so all positions process in one batch.
cards.hook: No GPU removes the generation loop

cards.front: A RAG answer is fluent but wrong. What is the first check?
cards.back: Is the correct source passage in the top-K retrieved results at all? Absent means a retrieval problem; present means a generation problem. One check halves the search space.
cards.hook: Top-K presence splits the space

cards.front: Traffic grows 100x. Name the levers in order, and the catch.
cards.back: Caching, batching, replicas, queuing — after locating the bottleneck. They interact: bigger batches raise throughput but latency, replicas raise cost, queuing adds wait.
cards.hook: Not "add more GPUs"

cards.front: Classify the failure before choosing a recovery. Why?
cards.back: Temporary (API timeout) gets bounded retries with backoff. Permanent (invalid input) makes retries pure waste — the workflow must take a different path.
cards.hook: Retrying invalid input forever

cards.front: Why does TTFT matter more than total completion in chat?
cards.back: The system feels fast if streaming starts quickly, even when the full answer is slow. Perception tracks first token, not last.
cards.hook: Perceived speed is the first token

cards.front: Latency for a chat product is which two numbers?
cards.back: TTFT — time to first token, driven by prefill and prompt size. TPS — tokens per second once streaming starts, driven by model size and GPU load. Different bottlenecks, different fixes.
cards.hook: "Measure latency" is a weak answer

cards.front: What is the counterintuitive result of decomposition?
cards.back: More steps with smaller models is often faster, cheaper and more accurate than one step with a big model — and each step is testable and localizable.
cards.hook: More steps, smaller models, better

cards.front: What is the last rung of the degradation ladder?
cards.back: Graceful handoff to a human with full context attached. Not an error page — the context is what makes the handoff worth anything.
cards.hook: Hand off with the context, not a 500

cards.front: Name the fallback for each failure class.
cards.back: Primary model down: secondary family, same contract. Invalid structured output: deterministic extraction or ask. Retrieval down: known-good cache or say you can't. Tool down: queue, alternative, or human.
cards.hook: Every critical path has a degraded mode

cards.front: Why is free-form text between LLM steps dangerous?
cards.back: It is the most common source of silent breakage: it works until the model phrases something differently, then produces plausible garbage instead of an exception.
cards.hook: It fails without failing

cards.front: McDonald's and IBM drive-thru voice ordering, June 2024.
cards.back: Ended after multi-year testing across roughly 100 locations, with widely-circulated videos of misinterpreted orders. Both framed it as a learning phase.
cards.hook: 100 locations, then discontinued

cards.front: The mistake behind most model-reliability incidents.
cards.back: Treating the model call as a function call rather than a network call to a system with variable latency, occasional outages and silent quality changes.
cards.hook: It is a network call, not a function

cards.front: What does an observability vendor imply about your data boundary?
cards.back: They are inside it, whether or not you thought about it. Redaction is part of the trace design, not a later privacy review.
cards.hook: Inside the boundary either way

cards.front: What is the standards-based path for agent tracing?
cards.back: OpenTelemetry with GenAI semantic conventions, or a dedicated LLM observability platform. Structured JSON with a trace id is enough only at prototype scale.
cards.hook: Conventions beat a bespoke schema

cards.front: What changes about tracing under regulation?
cards.back: Immutable audit trail, defined retention, access logging on the traces themselves, and documented redaction. The traces become regulated data.
cards.hook: Log who read the logs

cards.front: Define reliability for an agentic system.
cards.back: The system behaving predictably even when the model does not. Predictability is a property of the code around the model, never of the model.
cards.hook: Predictable despite an unpredictable part

cards.front: What is the sampling rule at production volume?
cards.back: Sample traces for cost, but always retain 100% of failures and escalations. Sampled-away failures are the ones you needed.
cards.hook: Sample the wins, keep every loss

cards.front: Schema-valid is not real — give the three examples.
cards.back: A date syntactically perfect and in the past. A device ID well-formed and nonexistent. A user ID valid and belonging to someone else. Semantic validation is a separate pass.
cards.hook: Well-formed, wrong, and accepted
cards.aryaka: A well-formed device ID that isn't on the customer's tenant is exactly this class.

cards.front: Name the six reliability mechanisms.
cards.back: Decomposition, contracts, validation, disciplined retries, fallbacks, and treating every model call as an unreliable upstream dependency.
cards.hook: Six mechanisms, none of them the model

cards.front: Which three components change in production without anyone calling it a deploy?
cards.back: Prompt version, model version and corpus snapshot. All three move quietly, and all three change behaviour.
cards.hook: Silent deploys, loud regressions

cards.front: What single question must a trace schema answer?
cards.back: Where did this fail? Design the schema backwards from that question, not from what is convenient to log.
cards.hook: One question, designed backwards

cards.front: The highest-leverage observability investment at maturity.
cards.back: A trace-to-eval-to-regression pipeline: a failed production trace becomes a test case with one click. That closes the loop between incident and prevention.
cards.hook: One click from incident to test

cards.front: Which trace block do teams skip, and what does it cost them?
cards.back: The versioning block. When quality drops on a Tuesday the first question is what changed — answerable only if every trace records prompt version, model version and corpus snapshot.
cards.hook: Three things move without a deploy

cards.front: The guardrail service itself is down. What happens?
cards.back: Read-only advisory paths fail open, logged loudly. Any write, external communication or customer-visible output fails closed to human handoff. Decide and approve this before the incident.
cards.hook: Under pressure someone decides wrongly

cards.front: The fastest source of guardrail improvement, that nobody uses.
cards.back: The false-positive log, reviewed weekly. And never hard-block silently: a blocked request needs a clear message, a path forward, and a log entry.
cards.hook: Nobody reads the block log

cards.front: The guardrail implementation ladder, cheapest first.
cards.back: Regex/deny-list (~0ms), classical fine-tuned classifier (5-30ms, underrated), small guard LLM like Llama Guard or ShieldGemma (100-400ms), managed service (100-500ms), full LLM judge (500-2000ms).
cards.hook: Classifiers are very good and very cheap

cards.front: A guardrail at 2% false-positive rate, 1M requests a month. What is the cost?
cards.back: 20,000 legitimate requests blocked — in support, 20,000 frustrated customers. False-positive rate is a product metric with an owner, not a security afterthought.
cards.hook: 2% is twenty thousand people
cards.aryaka: At our ticket volume a 2% false block is a daily stream of customers told no for nothing.

cards.front: How do experienced teams tune guardrail thresholds?
cards.back: Per action class. High recall — accept false positives — for DESTRUCTIVE actions; high precision — accept misses — for advisory read-only paths. One global threshold is wrong at both ends.
cards.hook: One threshold is wrong twice

cards.front: Guards naively add 400-1,000ms. Four ways to claw it back.
cards.back: Run independent guards in parallel with each other; run input guards in parallel with retrieval and cancel the model call if one trips; cheap tiers first, escalate only ambiguous cases; async log-and-alert for low-risk categories.
cards.hook: Parallel with retrieval, not before it

cards.front: Guardrails sit in three places. Name them and what each catches.
cards.back: Input (jailbreaks, injection, off-topic, PII in), output (ungroundedness, PII leakage, policy statements, format), action (unauthorized action, out-of-policy parameters, blast radius).
cards.hook: Three placements, three different jobs

cards.front: Name the managed guardrail platforms, and why naming them matters.
cards.back: Google Cloud Model Armor, Bedrock Guardrails, Azure Content Safety. Naming products correctly is a low-cost, high-value credibility signal — use them when you want the compliance story without owning the models.
cards.hook: Cheap credibility, correctly named

cards.front: Which guardrail class is actually load-bearing for safety?
cards.back: Action guardrails. Input and output guards are probabilistic quality controls that reduce probability; action guardrails are deterministic authorization that reduces possibility.
cards.hook: Probability versus possibility

cards.front: The line that separates guardrails from authorization.
cards.back: "Content guardrails are probabilistic and I expect them to fail some percentage of the time. Anything where failure is unacceptable goes in the deterministic policy layer in front of the tool."
cards.hook: Say it in one breath

cards.front: How does an architect resolve the streaming-guardrail trade-off?
cards.back: By consequence class, and by surfacing it rather than deciding alone: stream optimistically for an internal assistant, buffer for anything customer-facing, and tell product the TTFT cost is the price of the guarantee.
cards.hook: Surface the trade-off, don't resolve it silently

cards.front: Streaming and output guardrails conflict. Name all three strategies.
cards.back: Buffer-and-check (safe, destroys TTFT), chunked windowed checking (good middle, can miss violations spanning boundaries, needs overlap), optimistic stream with retraction (best latency, user may briefly see bad content).
cards.hook: You cannot un-send a token

cards.front: Two policy docs disagree — three remote days versus two. What does the agent do?
cards.back: Never pick randomly. Resolve by version, timestamp and authority metadata; if still unresolved, state the disagreement explicitly rather than choosing a side.
cards.hook: An arbitrary pick is unauditable

cards.front: Where does injection detection rank among defenses?
cards.back: Additional, never primary. Attackers rewrite around simple detectors. The controls that hold are server-side validation of every tool call and least privilege.
cards.hook: A detector is a filter, not a boundary

cards.front: Memory is a source of what, exactly?
cards.back: Context, not truth. Preferences change and facts expire, so memory needs last-updated metadata, validation before use, and forgetting — expire old, low-confidence and contradictory entries.
cards.hook: Stored once is not still correct

cards.front: Multi-tenant isolation has five boundaries. Which is new in agentic systems?
cards.back: Tool isolation. Data, access, compute and cache isolation are familiar; one tenant's agent reaching another's APIs, files or actions is the agentic addition.
cards.hook: Five boundaries, one of them new
cards.aryaka: A per-tenant agent must not reach another customer's MyAryaka endpoints — a fifth boundary beyond data and cache.

cards.front: Define the confused deputy in agent terms.
cards.back: The agent acts with its own high privilege on behalf of a low-privilege user — it runs as a broad service account and the permission check on the end user was never done.
cards.hook: Your service account, their request

cards.front: Where does delimiting untrusted content sit among the defenses?
cards.back: First and weakest: necessary, not sufficient. It reduces accidental instruction-following; it does not stop a deliberate attacker.
cards.hook: Necessary, never sufficient

cards.front: How should an agent's permissions be defined?
cards.back: Derive them from the identity system you already audit — the Salesforce and Microsoft pattern. New parallel permission models are where privilege escalation lives.
cards.hook: Never invent a second permission system

cards.front: State the dual-channel rule for high-risk agents.
cards.back: Reading untrusted content, holding private data, and being able to communicate externally is a complete exfiltration path. Break at least one leg.
cards.hook: Three legs make an exfiltration path
cards.aryaka: The portal copilot reads untrusted uploads and sees tenant data — so it gets no send capability at all.

cards.front: Name the attack surface.
cards.back: Direct injection, indirect injection, tool poisoning, unsafe output execution, excessive agency, data exfiltration, supply chain, confused deputy.
cards.hook: Eight vectors, one of them dominant

cards.front: Define excessive agency, with the canonical example.
cards.back: The agent can do more than the task requires — an agent that only needs to read tickets holding write access. Replit's production deletion was blast radius, not intent.
cards.hook: Blast radius is set by the credential

cards.front: The one question to ask of every agent design.
cards.back: If this were fully compromised right now, what is the worst it could do? If the answer is unacceptable, no prompt will fix it — reduce the permissions.
cards.hook: Unacceptable answer means fewer permissions

cards.front: Why is indirect injection the one to worry about most?
cards.back: It needs no contact with your system. The attacker just puts text where your agent will eventually read — a ticket, a shared doc, an inbound email, a scraped page, a log line.
cards.hook: They never have to talk to you
cards.aryaka: Every inbound ticket, attached config and customer email is a delivery channel.

cards.front: Which defense is the actual control, and why?
cards.back: Least privilege. The credential the agent holds is the security boundary and the only one that cannot be talked out of. Per-tool credentials, per-tenant scoping, short-lived tokens, read-only by default.
cards.hook: Permissions are guarantees; prompts are suggestions

cards.front: What must never happen to model output?
cards.back: No eval, no shell interpolation, no raw SQL. Parameterized queries, allow-listed commands, sandboxes. Generated code runs isolated: no network, no credentials, resource cap.
cards.hook: Parameterize, allow-list, sandbox

cards.front: What does output filtering catch that nothing else does?
cards.back: Leaked secrets, PII, unsafe links and policy violations on the way out. Cheap, and it is the only layer positioned after the model has already been wrong.
cards.hook: The last cheap layer

cards.front: Which OWASP LLM Top 10 entries account for most enterprise incidents?
cards.back: Prompt injection, insecure output handling, excessive agency, and sensitive information disclosure. Run the design against the list formally, not from memory.
cards.hook: Four of ten carry the incidents

cards.front: Why is a one-time pentest insufficient for injection?
cards.back: It is a snapshot of a moving target. Injection tests belong in the eval suite as permanent regression cases, and every published technique becomes a new case.
cards.hook: Every new technique is a test case

cards.front: The Samsung leak, 2023 — what was missing?
cards.back: A policy on what may cross into a third-party model provider. The failure was a data-boundary decision nobody had made, not a model behaviour.
cards.hook: No policy is a policy

cards.front: Microsoft Tay, 2016 — the enduring lesson.
cards.back: Untrusted input became system behavior because there was no boundary between content the system consumes and content that shapes it. Every indirect injection today is the same error, more sophisticated.
cards.hook: Racist output inside 24 hours

cards.front: State the agentic threat model in one line.
cards.back: Every input that reaches the model is attacker-controlled until proven otherwise; every output from the model is untrusted until validated.
cards.hook: Both directions untrusted by default

cards.front: What is tool poisoning?
cards.back: A tool returning attacker-influenced data — an API response carrying injected instructions, or a third-party MCP server's tool descriptions.
cards.hook: The tool's output is input too

cards.front: What turns injection from harder into ineffective?
cards.back: Deterministic validation before every consequential action. An injected instruction to refund $50,000 fails at the policy check regardless of how cleverly it was phrased.
cards.hook: Phrasing cannot pass a policy check

cards.front: Which abstractions are worth building on day one anyway?
cards.back: Idempotency keys, observability, tenant isolation, cost tracking, eval set. Proven patterns whose retrofit costs 10x abstract early; speculative patterns wait for the Rule of Three.
cards.hook: Proven-plus-expensive-to-retrofit outranks the Rule of Three.

cards.front: No adoption plan. Predict the adoption rate.
cards.back: 10-20%. AI features launch at 30-50% and stall there without training, workflow redesign, success metrics and exec sponsorship. A detailed 90-day plan gets you 60-80%.
cards.hook: "If we build it they will come" costs you forty points.

cards.front: Which of the three AI-vision questions matters most?
cards.back: The third: what will we deliberately NOT do with AI. Outcomes and capabilities are easy; the refusals are what prevent AI-washing. A good vision names them — customer-facing chat, sales outreach, regulated code generation.
cards.hook: "Leverage AI to drive innovation" decides nothing.
cards.aryaka: Write Aryaka's three refusals into the one-page vision before the CoE picks its next use case.

cards.front: The AI-spend thresholds that decide build, buy, or partner.
cards.back: Under $100K/year: buy. $100K-$500K/year: buy, plus build the agent layer. Over $500K/year: build, buy infrastructure, partner for narrow gaps. Recalibrate annually as vendor pricing moves.
cards.hook: Three numbers end a six-week strategy debate.
cards.aryaka: Aryaka's copilot spend sits in the middle band — buy the gateway and tracing, build the agent logic.

cards.front: Who can pull each kill-switch tier unilaterally?
cards.back: On-call SRE pulls Tier 1. On-call PM pulls Tier 2. Only the incident commander pulls Tier 3. Lower tiers move fast; higher tiers require concurrence and deliberation.
cards.hook: Speed at the bottom, human deliberation at the top.
cards.aryaka: Name the on-call SRE and PM for the copilot before launch, not during the incident.

cards.front: The five triggers that fire a kill switch, with thresholds.
cards.back: Hallucination over 5% sustained one hour; cost over 3x baseline sustained four hours; any confirmed PII leak; CSAT down over one point for 24 hours; any regulator or legal complaint.
cards.hook: Thresholds are starting points — calibrate to your own baseline.

cards.front: Name the three kill-switch tiers and their reversal times.
cards.back: Tier 1 degrade — cheaper model or non-AI path, reversible under 5 minutes. Tier 2 pause — no new sessions, in-flight completes, under 30 minutes. Tier 3 kill — abort everything, under 4 hours.
cards.hook: Degrade, pause, kill — 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 4 hours.

cards.front: Which kill-switch trigger skips the tiers entirely?
cards.back: Trigger 5. A regulator, legal or compliance complaint invokes Tier 3 immediately, regardless of operational state. Triggers 1 through 4 are operational and use the tiered response.
cards.hook: Legal does not get a degrade option.

cards.front: Where do most AI organizations stall, and for how long?
cards.back: Stage 1 to Stage 2 — pilot to platform — for 12-18 months. It requires leadership to fund infrastructure that ships no features. Teams do not form without a platform, and the platform does not form without teams.
cards.hook: The chicken-and-egg that eats a year and a half.
cards.aryaka: Aryaka sits at late Stage 1 / early Stage 2 — the stall risk is live right now.

cards.front: "Which model are we using?" Replace that question with what?
cards.back: "What's our eval set, our gateway, our prompt versioning, our observability?" A team that answers those four in detail barely needs the model choice. A team that cannot will not be saved by any model.
cards.hook: Frontier models are within 5% of each other.

cards.front: In build/buy, what are you never allowed to build?
cards.back: Your own agent framework, your own observability, your own model serving. LangGraph, Langfuse and vLLM exist. Build on top of those layers, never below them.
cards.hook: Differentiation lives above the layer, never below it.

cards.front: The AI org arc, its two triggers, and why you can't skip.
cards.back: CoE → platform team → embedded AI engineers, over 3-5 years. Trigger one: 5+ use cases and the CoE is the bottleneck. Trigger two: 50+ use cases. Skipping Stage 2 fails — embedded engineers need shared infrastructure to build on.
cards.hook: Each transition requires the central team to give up power.

cards.front: Five phrases that lose the room, and their replacements.
cards.back: "We'd add guardrails" → name placement, tier, false-positive cost. "Just use a vector DB" → chunking, hybrid, rerank, eval. "The model handles that" → model proposes, code validates. "Fully autonomous" → give a range and a fallback.
cards.hook: Nobody experienced says 100% accuracy.

cards.front: Four framing lines that mark you as senior in the first minute.
cards.back: "The question that determines everything is the blast radius of a wrong action." "I'd pick the least autonomous architecture that solves it." "That's a business rule, so it goes in code, not a prompt." "Let me name what I'd cut."
cards.hook: Two or three well-placed beat ten recited.

cards.front: The staffing ratio and the four ways a platform team dies.
cards.back: One platform engineer per 8-12 product engineers. It dies as gatekeeper (fix: policy-as-code in CI), consulting firm (synthesize, don't queue), tech-debt dump (own shared infra only), or pet-project lab (10% time, not 50%).
cards.hook: Below 1:12 it bottlenecks; above 1:8 it over-builds.
cards.aryaka: At ~30 engineers, three platform engineers is the right target.

cards.front: The post-incident clock after a kill switch is pulled.
cards.back: 24 hours root-cause published; 72 hours mitigation plan; one week customer comms; two weeks full post-mortem in eng review. The feature stays at its invoked tier until mitigation deploys.
cards.hook: Average response time with the framework: eight minutes.

cards.front: Five signals you are prematurely abstracting.
cards.back: Framework with one use case; config options for hypothetical needs; interfaces before two implementations; platform team before three product teams; designing for 100x at 1x volume.
cards.hook: Senior engineers enjoy building frameworks — that is the danger.

cards.front: Three principal-level sentences about cost, ownership, and risk.
cards.back: "This needs an owner for eighteen months; if we can't name them, we shouldn't start." "The build is cheap — the eval set and on-call load are the expense, and neither is in this estimate." "The business should own the autonomous-send risk decision explicitly."
cards.hook: Assign the risk; don't resolve it silently.

cards.front: Six warning signs an AI project is heading toward failure.
cards.back: No articulable eval set; model-choice talk crowding out system design; P95 untracked or over 5s; security review scheduled after launch; adoption plan is "the all-hands"; vendor pilot skipped.
cards.hook: Count them. Over three is a failure-mode inventory, not a roadmap.

cards.front: When are you allowed to abstract?
cards.back: Not before three concrete instances. First built specifically, second by copy-and-modify, third reveals what is stable and what varies — and that is the abstraction surface.
cards.hook: The framework emerges from the third agent, not the first.

cards.front: Leadership says build the platform first. Say what, verbatim?
cards.back: "We have one use case; the right abstraction is revealed by the third. Build the first directly, the second by copy-modify, and abstract at the third." Frame it as disciplined platform thinking.
cards.hook: Not anti-platform — anti-guessing.

cards.front: What separates senior, staff and principal in a design conversation?
cards.back: Senior: correct architecture, handles obvious failures. Staff: trade-offs with numbers, designs the eval and cost model, names what to cut. Principal: reframes the problem, questions whether to build it at all.
cards.hook: Staff names the cut; principal questions the build.

cards.front: The vendor demoed 95% accuracy. What will you actually get?
cards.back: 70-80%. Demos are tuned to their test data; your data is messier. Ask for the smallest 30-day pilot that validates the claim on your data — if they refuse to support one, walk away.
cards.hook: If the pilot fails, the demo was theater.

cards.front: Four vendor terms you never accept, whatever the score.
cards.back: No written data-export commitment; no audit log of who accessed your data; single-region only; proprietary fine-tuning format only they can serve. Each one makes your investment hostage.
cards.hook: Score the other dimensions — these four are refusals.

drills.title: Tier-1 wants an agent to route tickets. Is routing an agent problem?
drills.problem: Assumption: ~8,000 tier-1 tickets a month arrive by email, portal and API. Today a rota decides which queue each goes to; misroutes cost roughly a day of latency. Leadership has asked for 'an AI agent that routes tickets intelligently'. You have last year's tickets with their final queue, and about 20 destination queues. The stated success metric is misroute rate. Someone has already built a proof of concept with a frontier model, a 900-token prompt describing all 20 queues, and a tool that writes the queue field. It works, costs about $0.04 a ticket, and takes 6 seconds. Tell me what you would actually ship.
assesses: Placing a problem on the autonomy spectrum instead of accepting the label
Recognising a classification problem wearing agent clothing
Cost and latency reasoning at 8,000/month
Knowing what an agent buys and when that is nothing
Handling the political dimension of saying 'not an agent'
skeleton: Name the shape: the control flow is known — read ticket, choose one of 20 labels, write a field.
Known control flow means workflow, not agent. Nothing here depends on what a previous step discovered.
So the leftmost point on the autonomy spectrum that works is a classifier, with an LLM step at most.
Baseline first: a fine-tuned or few-shot small model on a year of labelled data, measured against the rota.
Route by confidence: high-confidence auto-routes, low-confidence goes to a human with the top two suggestions.
Reserve the frontier tier for the residual — the ambiguous and multi-intent tickets, which are the expensive ones.
Keep the tool write behind idempotency and an audit record; a misroute must be traceable and reversible.
Say the yes: an agent earns its place later, when the task becomes investigate-then-decide rather than label.
Frame it to leadership as sequencing, not refusal — same metric, cheaper, and it becomes the agent's router later.
numbers: $0.04 × 8,000 = ~$320/month for the frontier PoC; a small-model classifier lands closer to $10-30
6s per ticket is invisible here — this is a queue write, not an interactive answer, so latency is not the lever
Cost is not the argument on its own at this volume; the argument is accuracy per dollar and testability
traps: Building the agent because the ask said agent. That is how you inherit cost and debugging pain for no benefit.
Refusing flatly. 'Not an agent' without an alternative that hits the same metric reads as obstruction.
Leading with the $320. It is small enough to be dismissed, and it is not the real problem — testability is.
Forgetting the confidence path. A classifier with no human route is a misroute machine at the tail.

followups.q: So we're not doing AI here?
followups.a: We are — a trained classifier is AI. What we are not doing is paying agent overhead for a labelling task. The agent conversation starts when routing needs investigation, like checking topology before deciding the queue.

followups.q: What would change your answer?
followups.a: If correct routing required gathering evidence first — pulling device state or change history to tell a network fault from a billing question — the control flow stops being known and an agent starts earning its cost.

decisions.over: An agent with a queue-write tool
decisions.because: The control flow is known in advance, so nothing depends on discovery. Agent overhead buys cost and debugging pain with no accuracy gain.

decisions.choice: Small model, fine-tuned on a year of labels
decisions.over: A frontier model with a 900-token prompt listing 20 queues
decisions.because: The labels already exist and the task is narrow and high-volume — exactly where a small model wins on cost and repeatability.

decisions.choice: Frontier tier for the low-confidence residual only
decisions.over: One tier for all tickets
decisions.because: The ambiguous tail is where misroutes actually come from; spending the expensive tier there and nowhere else is the whole cascade argument.

drills.title: Design the approval surface for 400 agent-proposed network changes a day
drills.problem: Aryaka's remediation agent now proposes changes: restart a tunnel, adjust a QoS policy, push a config stanza. Volume is 400 proposals a day across three shifts and eight approvers. The current UI shows agent wants to act, approve or reject, and the approval rate is 99%. Two bad changes went through last month because nobody could see what would actually change. Leadership wants throughput to keep rising without the gate becoming theatre. You are asked to design the approval surface, the policy that decides what needs a human at all, and the metrics that tell you the gate is real.
assesses: Recognising approval theatre and knowing the metric that exposes it
Deriving the gate from an action class instead of asking per action
Designing the artifact a human can actually judge in seconds
Binding an approval to the exact proposal to prevent substitution
Queue economics: approver throughput as a system constraint
skeleton: Lead with the diagnosis: a 99% approval rate means the gate controls nothing and is costing eight people's attention.
Classify every action READ, WRITE_LOW, WRITE_HIGH, DESTRUCTIVE, and derive the gate from the class.
Auto-approve inside deterministic bounds; reserve humans for out-of-bounds and destructive classes.
Show the concrete artifact: the diff against the running config, blast radius, and the evidence behind the proposal.
Bind approval to a proposal hash so what executes is exactly what was shown.
Validate deterministically before the gate — policy lint, reachability simulation, refs exist, confidence threshold.
Make the queue a first-class surface: SLA on review time, alert on depth, auto-escalate on breach.
Instrument confirmation compliance, approval rate, time-to-decide, and post-approval failure rate.
Pair the gate with commit-confirm so an approved-but-wrong change self-reverts.
numbers: Approval rate above 95% means the gate is not functioning — 99% is the finding, not the baseline (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §20).
Throughput: 400 proposals/day at 30-60 seconds review is 200-400 minutes, roughly 3.5-6.5 approver-hours a day (issue 004, §19).
Auto-approving the 70% that fall inside deterministic bounds leaves 120 proposals and ~1-2 approver-hours (Assumption: bounds coverage modelled from the WRITE_LOW share).
Self-healing backstop: commit-confirm with an auto-rollback timer reverts a bad push in 120 seconds (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §9).
traps: Adding more approvers to fix the queue instead of removing the proposals that never needed a human.
Asking for approval with a natural-language summary and no diff — that is what produced the two bad changes.
Letting the agent re-plan after approval, so the executed action differs from the approved artifact.
Treating the HITL surface as a UI feature rather than an abstraction seam with sync, async and webhook backends.

followups.q: Approvers say the diff is too technical to judge at 3am. What changes?
followups.a: Pair the diff with the deterministic pre-flight result: syntax parse, policy lint, reachability simulation, and what rolls back automatically. The human decides on evidence and blast radius, not on reading config. If they still cannot judge, the action class is wrong for a human gate.

followups.q: How do you know the gate is working three months later?
followups.a: Confirmation compliance should be 100%, approval rate well under 95%, time-to-decide flat, and unauthorized-action attempts logged as a signal. A rising time-to-decide means the queue is the bottleneck and auto-approval bounds need widening on evidence.

followups.q: Who can bypass the gate in an incident?
followups.a: Nobody bypasses it; the kill switch replaces it. Tier 1 degrade is unilateral for on-call SRE, Tier 2 pause needs PM concurrence, Tier 3 kill needs the incident commander — and it works without a deploy.

decisions.over: Approve-everything, or a single confidence threshold
decisions.because: A flat gate produces a 99% approval rate — theater. Classing by side effect puts human attention only where blast radius justifies it.

decisions.over: An ML confidence score deciding what needs a human
decisions.because: Bounds are auditable and testable; a confidence score is neither, and it fails silently when the model drifts.

decisions.choice: Approval bound to a proposal hash
decisions.over: Approving an intent and re-planning at execution
decisions.because: Without the hash, what executes is not what was shown — the reviewer approved a different change.

decisions.over: Trusting the approval as the last line of defence
decisions.because: Approved-but-wrong still happens. A change that self-reverts unless confirmed bounds the damage to one confirm window.

drills.title: Design the cache stack for a copilot where a stale answer causes a customer outage
drills.problem: The support copilot answers questions like why is my tunnel flapping using runbooks plus live device state. Cost is $0.31 per ticket and the team wants it halved. The complication: last month a semantically cached answer told an engineer a threshold that had changed in the config two days earlier, and the site was black-holed for 20 minutes. Product now says any cache that can serve a stale operational fact is off the table. You are asked for the layered cache design, what each layer is allowed to cache, and how invalidation actually works.
assesses: Distinguishing five cache layers with different semantics and invalidation rules
Understanding that the invalidation model, not the hit rate, decides what may be cached
Separating stable-knowledge caching from live-state caching
Provenance tracking as a design requirement, not a feature
Quantifying savings honestly per layer
skeleton: Split the question space first: stable knowledge is cacheable, live operational state is not.
Start with the prompt cache — stable prefix first, variable last — highest hit rate, lowest risk.
Add the embedding cache keyed by content hash plus model id; it is deterministic and cannot go stale.
Tool result cache with per-tool TTL: seconds for live metrics, minutes for config snapshots, forever for historical events.
Response cache only for context-free queries; tag entries with tenant and invalidate on tenant config change.
Semantic cache last, and only with provenance: entry maps to source doc ids and evicts when they change.
Every key carries tenant_id — a cross-tenant cache hit is a security incident, not a cost win.
Sample cache hits continuously for human audit; without sampling you learn from the customer.
One invalidation event bus: any knowledge artifact publishes changed, all subscribed layers evict.
numbers: Layer hit rates and savings: L3 prompt 80-95% at 90% input discount; L5 embedding 60-90% at 100%; L4 tool 40-70%; L2 semantic 25-40%; L1 result 5-15% (issue 003, §5).
Tightening the semantic threshold from 0.95 to 0.98 cuts hit rate 35% to 15% and savings from $8K to $3.5K a month (issue 003, §12).
Embedding cache math: 1K tokens costs ~$0.0001, so $500/year becomes $50K/year if you re-embed 100 docs per query — a 100x sink (issue 004, §5).
Prompt cache TTL is 5-60 minutes, so low-traffic features need a warmer calling the prefix every 4 minutes (issue 004, §5).
traps: Quoting a semantic hit rate as the win without naming the invalidation model — that is the incident you just had.
Caching answers that embed live state at all; time-bound aggressively or serve uncached for freshness.
Omitting tenant_id from a key to raise the hit rate.
Shipping the semantic layer before the response and tool layers work — it is a v2, not a v1.

followups.q: Finance wants the $8K a month back. What do you tell them?
followups.a: We keep the savings that cannot be wrong: prompt, embedding, tool result and context-free response caching already move the bill more than the semantic layer did. The semantic layer returns once entries carry source doc ids and evict on document change — three weeks of work.

followups.q: The semantic cache worked fine at 1,000 queries a day. Why did it break at 100,000?
followups.a: The query distribution widened. More near-misses cross a fixed similarity threshold, so false positives scale faster than traffic. Mitigations are per-tenant namespaces, progressive threshold tightening as volume grows, and continuous sampling of hits for audit.

followups.q: Where does the cache stack stop helping cost?
followups.a: When the cheapest lever is structural, not cached: eliminate the call, gate scope at ingress, route tiers. Model routing is a 5-20x swing versus caching's 50-90% on input tokens only.

decisions.over: One cache TTL for the whole response
decisions.because: The question space is mixed: runbook explanations are stable, device state is not. One TTL either wastes savings or serves an outage.

decisions.choice: Prompt cache first, semantic cache last
decisions.over: Leading with the semantic cache because it saves the most
decisions.because: Prompt caching is 50-90% off input with no staleness risk. Semantic caching is where the stale-fact incident comes from — earn it last.

decisions.choice: Provenance-linked entries evicted on source change
decisions.over: Event-driven invalidation on knowledge-base update
decisions.because: Issue 011's incident: the KB update fired no event for semantically-near entries. Mapping entries to source doc ids makes eviction mechanical.

decisions.over: Tenant filtering at read time
decisions.because: A cross-tenant cache hit is a security incident, not a cost win — and it never raises an error.

drills.title: Design a model cascade that cannot exceed twelve cents per resolved ticket
drills.problem: Aryaka's copilot handles 1,000 tickets a day heading to 10,000 over 18 months. Naive frontier-only capacity math came to about $82K a month and the CFO approved a program on the condition that unit cost lands at $0.12 per resolved ticket or below, measured monthly. Resolution rate must stay above 60% and p95 first response under 5 seconds. Today there is one frontier model, one prompt, and no per-tenant ceiling. You are asked to design the cascade, prove the arithmetic, and say what happens on the day the ceiling is about to break.
assesses: Building a cost model before an architecture and defending it out loud
Tiering steps by required judgement rather than by model brand
Keeping a quality floor while cutting cost, with an explicit measurement plan
Enforcing a ceiling as a runtime control, not a dashboard
Naming what the extra spend buys when the frontier tier is used
skeleton: Build the ten-line cost model first: calls per ticket, tokens per call, price per token, tickets per month.
Tier the steps: rules and lookups at T0, classification and rewriting on a small model, judgement on frontier.
Ask the elimination question per step — can deterministic code do this at all?
Gate scope at ingress so out-of-scope tickets never reach the expensive reasoning step.
Layer the savings in order: routing, prompt caching, output caps, context trimming, then retrieval caching.
Instrument cost per successful task, cost by tenant, cost by intent, cache hit rate, and cost of failed runs.
Enforce the ceiling in the request path: cost-budget tokens per tenant per day, checked before the call.
On breach, degrade rather than refuse: cheaper tier, then queue-and-async, then cached response with a flag.
Tie the frontier tier to a named benefit per intent, reviewed monthly against resolution rate.
numbers: Baseline: 1,000 tickets x 5 calls x 50K tokens = 250M tokens/day; at $5/1M in and $15/1M out on a 70/30 split that is ~$2,750/day, about $82K/month (issue 004, §19).
Savings ladder: prompt caching cuts 40-60% to $35-50K; cascading half the calls cuts ~30% to $25-35K; self-hosted triage tier cuts ~20% to $20-28K/month (issue 004, §19).
Unit cost check: $24K/month over 30,000 tickets = $0.80 per ticket, so hitting $0.12 needs call count down from 5 and the small-model share up, not just caching.
Cost of failed runs is routinely 20-40% of spend in immature systems — the cheapest line to cut first (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
traps: Presenting a percentage saving with no absolute per-ticket number the CFO can hold you to.
Cascading by moving every worker to a cheap model and calling the quality risk acceptable without an eval.
A ceiling that only alerts: the $40K incident had an alert paged four hours before anyone acted.
Optimising efficiency before reliability — the most common sequencing error, because cost is visible and reliability is not.

followups.q: A vendor cuts frontier pricing 70%. Do you rip out the cascade?
followups.a: No. The answer is never switch to B, it is add B as a cascade tier and measure. Price cuts change tier boundaries, not the architecture; the cascade is what lets you absorb the change in config instead of a rewrite.

followups.q: Resolution rate drops two points after the cascade lands. What do you do?
followups.a: Check per-segment eval scores, not the aggregate — model swaps hide long-tail regressions. Promote the affected intents back to the higher tier, keep the rest cheap, and let the error budget decide whether the ceiling or the quality SLO gives.

followups.q: Where does the per-tenant ceiling actually live?
followups.a: In the gateway as a Redis counter of cost-budget tokens computed at request time from token count times model rate, atomic with Lua. A $100/day tenant holds 100,000 tokens; a $0.50 reasoning request consumes 500.

decisions.choice: Deterministic code at T0 before any model tier
decisions.over: Routing everything to a small model first
decisions.because: The elimination question comes before the routing question: a lookup or regex answers some steps at zero marginal cost and 100% reliability.

decisions.choice: Cost-budget tokens per tenant per day, checked pre-call
decisions.over: A monthly spend alert on the provider dashboard
decisions.because: Alerts are post-hoc — issue 003 burned $40K in four hours. A pre-call check makes the ceiling a property of the system.

decisions.choice: Degrade on breach (cheaper tier, then async, then cached)
decisions.over: Hard-refusing the request at the ceiling
decisions.because: Refusal turns a cost control into an outage for the tenant. Degradation keeps the SLO honest and the bill bounded.

decisions.choice: Frontier tier justified per intent, reviewed monthly
decisions.over: A blanket 'complex tickets get the frontier model' rule
decisions.because: Without a named benefit per intent, the expensive tier expands by default and the cascade quietly stops saving anything.

drills.title: The agent proposes a config push. Prove it cannot land inside someone else's change window.
drills.problem: Assumption: the config-change agent proposes roughly 400 changes a day across 500 tenants, and a human approves each. Last quarter two approved changes landed during a customer's frozen window and one collided with a concurrent tier-3 maintenance, taking down a site for 20 minutes. The approvers cannot hold 500 change calendars in their heads. Change windows live in the change-management system, some tenants keep theirs in email, and tier-3's maintenance schedule is a separate calendar. Design the guard. Assume you cannot make the tenants change how they record windows this quarter.
assesses: Turning a human-judgement failure into a deterministic pre-condition
Designing around authoritative-source gaps you cannot fix
Fail-closed versus fail-open reasoning on a safety check
Making the check visible in the approval artifact
Handling the race between approval and execution
skeleton: Reframe: this is not an approval-quality problem, it is a missing deterministic pre-condition.
The guard runs before the change is ever shown to a human — an ineligible change never reaches the queue.
Build one window resolver over three sources: change-management records, tier-3 calendar, tenant-specific overrides.
Where a tenant's window only exists in email, the resolver returns unknown — and unknown fails closed, not open.
Fail-closed on unknown is the whole design: an unverifiable window blocks and routes to a human to confirm.
Re-check at execution, not only at proposal — approval and execution are separated by minutes to hours.
Bind the approval to the resolved window plus the proposal hash, so a changed window invalidates the approval.
Surface it in the artifact: the approver sees the window, its source, and its freshness, not just the diff.
Instrument the gap: count unknown-window proposals per tenant and publish it — that report is what fixes the data.
Pair with commit-confirm so a change that lands wrong reverts without a human in the loop.
numbers: 400 proposals a day against 500 calendars is why this cannot be a human check — it is a lookup
Two breaches and one collision in a quarter is roughly a 1-in-6,000 event rate; fail-closed trades throughput for that tail
The unknown-window count per tenant is the metric that drives the data cleanup, so publish it monthly
traps: Adding the change calendar to the prompt and asking the model to check. That is prompt-as-policy on a safety control.
Failing open when the window is unknown, because blocking is inconvenient. Unknown is exactly the case that caused the incident.
Checking only at proposal time, leaving the approval-to-execution gap the collision actually happened in.
Reporting a single collision count. Without the unknown-window-by-tenant breakdown, nobody fixes the source data.

followups.q: Fail-closed will block changes every day. Operations will hate it.
followups.a: It blocks only proposals whose window cannot be resolved, and the per-tenant count tells you where. That report is the lever that gets windows into the system — the friction is pointed at the cause.

followups.q: Why re-check at execution if the approver just looked?
followups.a: Because the window can change in the gap, and the approval was for a state that no longer holds. Binding approval to the resolved window plus proposal hash makes a stale approval fail instead of executing.

decisions.choice: A deterministic window resolver as a pre-condition
decisions.over: Adding calendars to the prompt for the model to check
decisions.because: A safety control that can be argued with is not a control. This is a lookup with a boolean answer.

decisions.choice: Fail closed on an unresolvable window
decisions.over: Proceeding when the window is unknown
decisions.because: Unknown is precisely the state that produced the incident; blocking converts a customer outage into an internal delay.

decisions.choice: Re-check at execution and bind approval to the window
decisions.over: Checking once at proposal time
decisions.because: Approval and execution are separated by minutes to hours, which is the gap the collision happened in.

decisions.over: Reporting only blocked-change totals
decisions.because: The totals justify the guard; the per-tenant breakdown is what actually gets the source data fixed.

drills.title: Design a 30-minute config-migration workflow that survives pod restarts and a mid-flight deploy
drills.problem: Aryaka is migrating 1,200 customer sites onto a new IPSec profile. Each site is a 20-30 minute workflow: pull running config, generate the new stanza, run pre-flight checks, stage to one device, verify, then proceed or roll back. Today it runs as an in-process LangGraph loop and there are 60-80 concurrent runs; last week an inference pod restart lost 34 in-flight migrations at minute 18. A platform deploy is scheduled mid-campaign. You are asked how you make this durable, what engine you pick, and how you migrate without a rewrite.
assesses: Knowing where in-process orchestration structurally ends
Durable execution concepts: checkpointing, replay, determinism, worker versioning
Choosing an engine on operating constraints rather than fashion
Handling in-flight workflows across a code change
Sequencing a migration under an active campaign
skeleton: State the wall: in-process breaks around 100 concurrent long-running workflows, and we are at 60-80.
Requirement is durable execution: state checkpointed after every step, resume from the last checkpoint on crash.
Externalise all state now: nothing in process memory beyond a single step; Redis ephemeral, Postgres durable, S3 blobs.
Pick on constraints: LangGraph checkpointer under 50 concurrent, Temporal if 1,000+ in 18 months, Inngest if under 500 and DX-led.
Ban non-deterministic workflow code — no clock or random calls outside captured state; enable the linters in CI.
Idempotency key per state-changing step from run id plus step index, so replay does not re-push a config.
Model the campaign as a saga: staged push, verify, compensate by auto-rollback if verification fails.
Worker versioning: in-flight runs finish on the old workflow version, new runs start on the new one.
Migrate strangler-fig behind a flag: cold paths first, 30% then 60% then 90%, decommission last.
numbers: Concurrency: 1,200 sites at 25 minutes each, 70 concurrent = 1,200 x 25 / 70 = ~430 minutes of wall clock, about 7 hours per full pass.
Failure cost today: a restart at minute 18 of a 20-minute run wastes 18 minutes of model spend per lost run, times 34 runs (issue 007, §5).
Scale thresholds to quote: 100 concurrent breaks in-process, 1,000 needs sharded workers by workflow id, 10,000 needs automated anomaly detection (issue 007, §5).
Self-healing window: commit-confirm with an auto-rollback timer means a bad push reverts in 120 seconds (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §9).
traps: Big-bang rewrite into Temporal mid-campaign — 2-3 quarters of migration compressed into a sprint.
Calling the LangGraph checkpointer a workflow engine: no replay, no multi-service coordination, no versioning.
Retrying a state-changing step without an idempotency key, which duplicates the config push.
Leaving conversation-as-state: without a typed persisted state object there is no resumability and no idempotency.

followups.q: The deploy lands mid-campaign anyway. What breaks?
followups.a: Nothing, if in-flight workflows pin the old workflow version and state is external. What breaks is non-deterministic workflow code: on replay it takes a different path and the run is corrupted. That is why the linter is CI-blocking, not advisory.

followups.q: Why not just extend the timeout and retry the whole site?
followups.a: A 30-minute retry is another 30 minutes of model spend and it re-executes side effects. Durable execution resumes at the last completed step; the cost of adding an engine late is 3-5x the cost of adding it early.

followups.q: What is the first signal that you have crossed the wall?
followups.a: The state store, not the app. Postgres-backed engines start degrading around 100 concurrent long-running workflows; before that you see memory pressure from held contexts at 50-200KB per workflow and blocked threads on tool timeouts.

decisions.over: LangGraph's Postgres checkpointer
decisions.because: The checkpointer is right under ~50 concurrent workflows; at 60-80 today and 1,000+ within 18 months, durable execution and worker versioning are the requirement.

decisions.over: Inngest
decisions.because: Inngest wins on developer experience under ~500 concurrent, but the 18-month projection and the need for in-flight version pinning favour Temporal.

decisions.over: A single database transaction across systems
decisions.because: The controller, ticketing and CRM cannot share a transaction. Explicit compensation per step is the only honest rollback.

decisions.choice: Idempotency key = run id + step index
decisions.over: A fresh UUID per attempt
decisions.because: A key that changes per attempt is not a key. Deterministic derivation is what makes a replay safe after a pod restart.

drills.title: Design the write path for an agent that touches ticketing, CRM, email and the controller
drills.problem: A resolution agent completes a ticket by doing four things: set ticket status resolved, email the customer, increment a KB article's helpful count, and close the case in the CRM. Two of the four APIs support an idempotency key; the KB service supports none. Last month a 500 that was actually a response timeout produced two Jira tickets for one bug, and the agent then updated both. You are asked to design the write path so that retries are safe and a mid-sequence failure leaves the system in a defined state.
assesses: Idempotency key derivation that survives retries and stays unique across steps
Choosing among idempotency patterns per API capability
Saga compensation design with explicit triggers
Retry discipline differentiated by error class
Verifying effects rather than trusting a 200
skeleton: Name the failure: a timeout is not a failure to write, so retry without a key creates duplicates.
Derive the key as run id plus step index plus tool name — deterministic across retries, unique across steps.
Never include timestamps or fresh UUIDs; the key must be a pure function of the logical operation.
Match the pattern to the API: header key where supported, deterministic operation id internally, ETag for read-modify-write.
For the KB service with no support, wrap it in an outbox: write intent, background worker dedupes.
Model the four steps as a saga with a compensation and a trigger per step.
Differentiate retries: transient infra backs off with jitter, malformed output repairs once, semantic errors escalate, business rejection branches.
Verify after write by read-back, and store the key beside the response in the trace store.
Test it: call every state-changing tool twice with one key and assert a single resource.
numbers: Retrofit economics: idempotency costs 1 engineer-week on day one versus 2-3 engineer-months later (issue 008, §18).
Observed cost of skipping it: 47 duplicate tickets in one hour, 2 days of cleanup, 6 engineering days against 1 day of prevention (issue 005, §18).
Retry shape: 3 attempts, exponential backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, jitter plus or minus 25% to avoid a thundering herd (issue 003, §7).
Timeout hierarchy that must compose: tool 5-15s inside step 30s inside run 90s inside worker 5min inside queue visibility 1h (issue 003, §7).
traps: One retry policy for all error types, which either burns money or hammers a struggling dependency.
Generating a new key on retry, which silently disables server-side dedupe.
Aborting mid-sequence with no compensation, leaving the customer emailed but the ticket open.
Reading the ticket back through the same cached tool result you just wrote.

followups.q: The email is already sent and step 4 fails. What is the compensation?
followups.a: Send a disregard-previous-email compensation and revert ticket status to open, triggered by the later failure. Compensation is not a rollback, it is a defined forward path to a consistent state; the saga orchestrator tracks step state and fires it.

followups.q: How do you catch an idempotency regression before production?
followups.a: Integration tests that call every state-changing tool twice with the same key and assert one resource created, plus the key recorded in the trace so duplicates are searchable. Document the derivation in the tool's MCP spec so new tools inherit it.

followups.q: Which of these four should the agent be allowed to do autonomously?
followups.a: Scope rigor to consequence, not volume. Ticket comment is reversible-write with audit and rate limits; the customer email is customer-visible and needs an output policy check or hard deterministic limits; anything touching config is approval, idempotency, rollback and kill switch.

decisions.choice: Deterministic key from run id + step index + tool
decisions.over: A UUID or timestamp per call
decisions.because: The key must be a pure function of the logical operation, or a retry after a timeout writes twice.

decisions.choice: Outbox wrapper for the KB service
decisions.over: Skipping idempotency where the API lacks support
decisions.because: The weakest API decides the failure mode. Writing intent first and deduping in a worker gives the guarantee the vendor doesn't.

decisions.choice: Retry classes differentiated by error type
decisions.over: One exponential-backoff policy for every failure
decisions.because: Retrying a business rejection is pointless and retrying a malformed output forever is issue 003's reflection loop. The class decides the response.

decisions.over: Trusting the 2xx response
decisions.because: Verification catches partial writes and eventual-consistency surprises across four systems that fail differently.

drills.title: Copilot traffic is about to grow 100x. Scale inference without a blank cheque.
drills.problem: Assumption: the support copilot serves ~800 requests a day today across 80 engineers, on hosted frontier models through the gateway. The plan is to expose it to all 500 customers' portals — call it 80,000 requests a day within two quarters, with the same p95 latency target and a cost ceiling that grows 10x, not 100x. You have provider rate limits, one self-hosted GPU tier for regulated tenants, and a queue you have not needed yet. Sequence the work and say what each lever costs you.
assesses: Locating the bottleneck before spending
Knowing the four levers and the order that wastes least money
That the levers interact rather than compose cleanly
Provider rate limits as the real ceiling, not GPUs
Choosing degradation over failure at the limit
skeleton: First locate it: model, GPUs, request rate, or the latency requirement. Scaling the wrong one buys nothing.
At 100x on hosted models the first wall is provider rate limits, not compute — so this is a queue-and-quota problem before it is a capacity problem.
Lever one, caching: prompt-prefix, retrieval results and repeated queries. Cheapest, and the query distribution is skewed enough to matter.
Lever two, batching: group requests arriving in the same window into one inference pass, which lifts GPU utilisation on the self-hosted tier.
Lever three, replicas behind a load balancer for parallel capacity — the lever that costs money linearly.
Lever four, queuing: buffer rather than drop when traffic exceeds capacity, with Retry-After and a job id.
Now say the interactions out loud: bigger batches raise throughput and latency; replicas raise capacity and cost; queuing protects the system and adds wait.
Protect the interactive path with bulkheads so portal traffic cannot starve engineer traffic.
Then the cheaper structural lever: cascade the easy 60% to a small model, which cuts the volume the expensive tier ever sees.
Instrument cost per successful task and the escalation rate, so the 10x ceiling is a measured constraint rather than a hope.
numbers: 800/day to 80,000/day is 100x volume against a 10x cost ceiling — a 10x improvement in cost per request is the actual requirement
Caching plus cascade is where that comes from; replicas alone scale cost linearly and fail the ceiling
Batching helps only the self-hosted tier; hosted endpoints already batch server-side, so do not claim it twice
traps: Reaching for GPUs first. On hosted models the ceiling is the rate limit, and retry storms against it make things worse.
Claiming caching and batching and replicas each cut cost 50% and multiplying them. They interact, and one of them raises latency.
Dropping requests at the limit instead of queuing with a job id and Retry-After.
Forgetting the cascade. It is the only lever that changes cost per request by an order of magnitude.

followups.q: Why not just raise the rate limit with the provider?
followups.a: That is worth doing and it is not a design. It moves the ceiling without changing cost per request, so the 10x budget still fails at 100x volume. The cascade and cache are what change the unit economics.

followups.q: Batching raises latency. How do you keep p95?
followups.a: Batch only the latency-tolerant paths — portal self-service and overnight work — and keep the engineer-facing path unbatched behind its own bulkhead. The window is a per-path setting, not a global one.

decisions.over: Adding replicas and GPU capacity first
decisions.because: Volume grows 100x against a 10x budget, so cost per request has to fall 10x. Replicas scale cost linearly and cannot deliver that.

decisions.over: Rejecting requests above capacity
decisions.because: A dropped request is an outage for that customer; a queued one with a job id and Retry-After is a slower success.

decisions.over: One global batching window
decisions.because: Batching trades latency for throughput, and the engineer-facing path is exactly where that trade is unacceptable.

decisions.choice: Bulkheaded pools for portal versus engineer traffic
decisions.over: One shared pool sized for peak
decisions.because: 500 customers' portal traffic will saturate a shared pool and starve the internal users who already depend on it.

drills.title: Every model call in the company must pass through one gateway you own — design it
drills.problem: Six teams at Aryaka call three providers directly with their own keys: the support copilot, NOC triage, a docs assistant, sales QBR summaries, a netops script generator, and one shadow project nobody registered. Finance cannot attribute last quarter's bill to a tenant, feature or team. Two teams pin no model snapshot. There is no fallback when a provider degrades. You are asked for a gateway that is mandatory, adds under 50ms, and does not become the org's bottleneck — plus the migration story for teams who will resist losing their keys.
assesses: Separating a data-plane choke point from a governance land grab
What must be enforced at the gateway versus left to the calling team
Cost attribution design that engineers cannot bypass
Provider failover and version pinning as platform primitives
Adoption strategy when the platform has no authority over the teams
skeleton: Define the contract first: one call signature, tags required, snapshot pinned, response carries cost and version.
Enforce at the gateway what must never vary: tags, per-tenant quotas, redaction, audit, snapshot resolution.
Inject tenant_id, feature_id, user_id, request_id from request-scoped context in a wrapper nobody calls around.
Resolve logical names to concrete snapshots from a registry; never let production call a floating alias.
Per-provider circuit breakers; open circuit routes to the secondary family under the same contract.
Layer the caches at the gateway: HTTP for tool and model catalogs, prompt cache prefix discipline, response cache for context-free queries.
Publish the gateway as a product: SDK, dashboards, cost per feature, and a one-PR swap for provider changes.
Adoption via the abstraction seam, not a mandate — first consumer is the copilot, then deprecate direct keys.
numbers: Attribution gap: unset per-model pricing in the trace store underreports cost 30-50%, so the gateway must stamp cost itself (issue 004, §9).
Failover budget: circuit trips at 5 consecutive failures or 50% over 30s, half-open after 60s — failover inside ~30s (issue 003, §7).
Cache economics at the gateway: prompt cache hits 80-95% with 90% input discount; add L1 response cache at 5-15% for 100% saving (issue 003, §5).
Scale of the bill being governed: 100k requests/month at ~10 model calls each is 1M model calls/month, where routing is a 10-20x swing (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
traps: Making the gateway a policy committee — if it adds a review step per call, teams route around it.
A wrapper that leaks provider-specific parameters in its signature: indirection, not a seam.
Owning prompts and orchestration at the gateway; that couples releases across six teams.
No fallback path behind the circuit breaker, so circuit-open equals total outage.

followups.q: A team says the gateway adds latency they cannot afford. What do you do?
followups.a: Measure it against the real budget: the external tool call is usually the largest component, and time-to-first-token matters more than total. If the gateway hop is material, give them streaming pass-through and a local cache, not an exemption from tagging and quotas.

followups.q: What do you deliberately not build in v1?
followups.a: No model-router abstraction until three models are in regular use, no multi-region abstraction until a customer requires it, no plugin marketplace. Cascade config is enough. The seams to build now are model client, tool registry, trace store, tenant config, HITL gateway.

followups.q: How do you find the shadow project?
followups.a: Provider-side key inventory plus an agent registry with owner, purpose, data classes, permission set and eval status per agent, and a review gate before anything gets write access. Ungoverned data flows are an enterprise-stage failure mode, not a rare one.

decisions.over: A policy mandate that all teams migrate
decisions.because: A mandate creates shadow keys. Making the gateway the easiest path — SDK, dashboards, one-PR provider swap — makes migration self-interested.

decisions.over: Letting services pin model versions themselves
decisions.because: Floating aliases are how quality changes arrive unannounced. Central resolution makes 'which model served this' answerable from the trace.

decisions.choice: Tags injected by a request-scoped wrapper
decisions.over: Asking callers to pass tenant and feature tags
decisions.because: Optional attribution is absent attribution — that is how a $180K bill becomes unexplainable.

decisions.choice: Per-provider circuit breakers with a secondary family
decisions.over: Retrying the primary provider harder during an outage
decisions.because: Retries against a degraded provider extend the outage and inflate the bill. A second family under the same contract is the only real fallback.

drills.title: Design tenant isolation for one shared vector index serving 500 SASE tenants
drills.problem: You own the retrieval layer of Aryaka's support copilot. 500 tenants, 12M chunks of runbooks, config stanzas and resolved tickets in one index with tenant_id in chunk metadata. Last quarter an internal test query returned another tenant's config diff; the filter was applied at 11 of 13 call sites. Retrieval budget is 600ms inside a 6s p95 response. The corpus grows to 40M chunks in 18 months, and three regulated tenants now demand EU-only processing. Leadership wants a design where a cross-tenant hit is structurally impossible, plus a migration path with no re-embedding downtime.
assesses: Whether isolation is enforced by architecture or by convention at each call site
Knowing vector search fails silently rather than erroring on a wrong partition
Trading physical isolation against operational cost across 500 tenants of different size
How isolation is proven — automated tests versus code review
Sequencing a live index migration without a re-embed outage
skeleton: Name the failure mode first: vector search returns plausible neighbours from the wrong partition, never an error.
Move enforcement into one shared retrieval client that no call site can bypass; tenant comes from request context.
Tier the tenants: shared index plus mandatory filter, per-namespace for large tenants, dedicated index for regulated.
Filter at query time, permission-aware; never post-filter, which leaks through result counts and latency.
Every chunk carries tenant, product, version, effective date, classification, source, permissions; every query filters the applicable set.
Extend tenant_id to cache keys, traces, and eval sets — a cross-tenant cache hit is the same incident.
Prove it with cross-tenant leakage cases in the CI eval suite, not by code review.
Migrate by dual-reading behind the client, backfilling namespaces incrementally, comparing recall, then cutting over.
numbers: Index size: 12M chunks at 1024 dims, ~4 GB per 1M vectors = ~48 GB today; 40M chunks = ~160 GB (issue 008, §2).
Dimensionality is a one-way door: re-embedding 10M documents costs ~$30K in API calls plus 2 weeks of pipeline work (issue 008, §2).
Latency: 600ms retrieval + 200ms rerank fits inside the 6,000ms p95 tool-using budget with ~950ms headroom (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
Retrofit economics: tenant isolation costs 1 engineer-week on day one versus 3-6 engineer-months later (issue 008, §18).
traps: Trusting per-call-site filters or a prompt instruction — one missed call site is the whole incident.
Post-filtering an unfiltered search: it still leaks through counts and timing, and you paid for the wrong search.
Giving all 500 tenants a dedicated index — operations cost explodes with no risk-based justification.
Deriving tenant_id from anything the model produced instead of the authenticated request context.

followups.q: A tenant wants proof, not assurances. What do you hand them?
followups.a: The cross-tenant leakage suite results from CI, the single retrieval client code path, per-tenant trace records carrying tenant_id, the gateway residency check that blocks and alerts on violation, and the quarterly residency audit.

followups.q: Does the EU-only tenant change the isolation model?
followups.a: Yes — logical becomes physical. A regional data plane owns inference, vector DB, trace store and conversation memory; the global control plane holds config only. For an EU-ONLY tenant, regional failure returns 503 rather than failing over across the boundary.

followups.q: How do you know the filter is working today, before the redesign lands?
followups.a: Add the leakage probes now and run them hourly against production namespaces. Also grep every retrieval call site and count them — 11 of 13 is a number you can only quote because someone audited. Instrument filters-applied in the trace retrieval block.

decisions.choice: Tiered isolation: filtered shared index, namespaces, dedicated for regulated
decisions.over: One dedicated index per tenant
decisions.because: 500 dedicated indexes is unmanageable and mostly unnecessary; the tier is chosen by tenant size and regulatory status, not uniformly.

decisions.choice: Enforcement inside one shared retrieval client
decisions.over: Trusting each call site to pass the filter
decisions.because: Issue 002's leak was one call path missing the filter. A client no call site can bypass makes the correct thing the only thing.

decisions.over: Post-filtering results after retrieval
decisions.because: Post-filtering leaks through result counts and latency, and silently degrades recall for the tenant that filtered most.

decisions.choice: Cross-tenant leakage cases in the CI eval suite
decisions.over: Code review and a pen test before GA
decisions.because: Retrofit security never arrives. A failing eval case is the only control that survives the next refactor.

drills.title: Design the answer path for "is it your network or my application?"
drills.problem: The single most contested ticket class a SASE provider handles. The customer says the app is slow; the provider's view says the underlay is healthy. Evidence lives in four places: path metrics (loss, latency, jitter per hop), tunnel and link state, the customer's own application telemetry which you may not have, and the change history on both sides.
